# Command, Preferences, and Package Version Interface Proposal

For this round, don't treat the entry points around the piano roll as one thing. Commands change project state, window selections look like preferences, and package information looks like the result of a read; although editing tools appear in the same interface, they may not share the same save timing as those three categories of objects.

An earlier investigation used `OpenUtau.Core/DocManager.cs` to reach the area around document state. The filename and nearby names can serve as a starting point, but they aren't enough to determine where commands are created, where package candidates enter the flow, or which object writes window settings back. Keep this entry point here without expanding it into an overall manager.

There are currently three options.

1. Keep the existing entry point and only add separate explanations for each object.
2. Add a read-only wrapper so the UI can get command, window, and package information through one name.
3. Merge window preferences and editing tools into a single editing state.

The first option is the tentative recommendation. It doesn't migrate existing callers or tie different lifecycles together just to make things easier to find. The second option only offers a shorter reading path; if the wrapper starts handling writes or choosing defaults on behalf of callers, its scope will expand. The third option is supported only by proximity in the UI, with no basis for shared state.

Don't start the trial by aggregating things. First check one small behavior in each category: whether executing a command allows a return to the pre-execution state; whether the window's form is retained when the piano roll is closed and reopened; whether multiple package candidates are handled according to their version text; and whether the base mode and pen tool variants can be tracked individually. If any check requires changing how existing callers use the interface, stop and record the issue beside the original entry point.

Still to fill in: where command group display names come from; whether there is already an established choice when a preference is missing; whether version candidates include preview entries; and whether tool categories and temporary override state are independent.

# Command, Preferences, and Package Version Interface Proposal

The initial review sheet grouped commands, window preferences, package versions, and piano roll tools together because maintainers often encounter them in sequence when tracing down from the editing UI. That order only indicates adjacent lookup paths, not shared state between the objects. The second revision made this explicit first: a sequence of UI actions is not a substitute for reference relationships.

An early draft considered a broader approach: add a unified wrapper between the UI and the existing objects. The wrapper would give readers a fixed starting point and could present the current window and tool in one place. But extending that idea to writes runs into different problems. Command changes need to preserve undo boundaries; window settings need to be observed across closing and reopening; package versions require a choice among candidate strings; and tools require a distinction between the base mode and pen tool variants. Compressing them into one return shape saves a lookup hop, but may mix together the reasons for failure.

This revision therefore no longer treats a "unified entry point" as the default direction. Keeping the original entry points and adding local notes remains the lower-cost option. If a caller is later found to need to read multiple kinds of information at once, a separate read-only adapter can be added. The adapter must not take over state writes or supply an unconfirmed default behavior for existing callers.

## Review Around the File

The review starts at `OpenUtau.Core/DocManager.cs`. Terms in the old notes that can help locate the relevant material include `track`, `ucommand`, `execute`, `ucommandgroup`, `docmanager`, and preference-related names. These are enough to get someone near document state, but cannot be assembled into a complete call graph.

The counterexample in this review is straightforward: following the UI steps first leads to tool switching in the piano roll; searching by object name first lands near commands or preferences. Both routes find local material, but they do not automatically converge. Declaring a common owner solely because the searches hit the same file would cause every creation site that cannot be found later to be incorrectly assigned to that file.

There was a working hypothesis: since these names appeared in the same search area, adding a wrapper might make later maintenance easier. The review did not support that inference. The matching locations are only navigation points; in particular, they do not explain where package version candidates feed in or all the creation paths for command groups. This revision drops that hypothesis and retains a narrower conclusion: the existing paths are suitable places to start looking, not a basis for assigning ownership to objects.

## Four Observation Tracks

The command track concerns only a single undoable state change. Choose an existing command and record the affected document state before execution, the changes after execution, and whether undo restores the original state. There is no need to redesign the command lifecycle here, nor to extrapolate from "can be undone" that all commands are created the same way. If the trial requires changing a synchronous action to wait for a callback, that exceeds the scope of entry-point documentation; stop that branch.

The preferences track looks only at whether the piano roll is displayed as a separate window. First change the window configuration, save and close it, then reopen it and check whether the displayed configuration matches the saved value. Tool switching, temporary modifier keys, and pitch categories are not part of this track. Even if they appear in the piano roll at the same time, they are not evidence of the window's attachment state. This round has no material that would justify setting a rule for callers on how to handle missing preferences.

The package version track observes only candidates that have already reached the entry point. At least three outcomes need to be distinguished: selection when there are multiple comparable candidates, the return when there are no usable candidates, and who should handle text that cannot be compared. Display order cannot be treated directly as version order. Whether registry preview entries participate in selection remains unconfirmed; this trial does not preemptively prescribe including or excluding them.

The tool track has two directions. The first looks at the externally exposed tool value from the base mode; the second looks at the current pen tool from the pen tool variant. This avoids incorrectly describing the "current tool" as a single persisted setting. The trial records only the mode, variant, and visible tool value before and after switching. If changing the window display also changes the tool value, record the trigger sequence first rather than immediately merging the state objects.

## Two Shortcuts Not Adopted

> Put commands, preferences, and package information into one service, then have the service return the complete editing state to the piano roll.

This excerpt from the old draft is retained because people have continued to look for the discussion under "unified service." It is not part of the trial. Synchronous state changes, persisted window settings, and candidate version selection have different failure paths, and tool modes should not automatically become preference fields. A unified appearance is not enough to establish that they should share a write boundary.

Another suggestion was to add a short alias for each entry point. This appears to reduce search cost, but once callers use the aliases, they become another set of long-term interfaces. Keeping the existing object names and file starting points is more appropriate at this stage. When a direct relationship cannot be found, record which object could not be found; do not hide the gap with a new name.

## Trial Stop Conditions

If adding a wrapper requires changing command undo semantics, stop; if restoring the window configuration requires also writing tool selection to preferences, stop; if a seemingly normal version string is filled in when there are no candidates, stop; if the base mode and pen tool variant can only be explained through the same field, stop and recheck the observation sequence.

This proposal commits only to local documentation and local observation at this point. It does not commit to building an overarching entry point or filling in all ownership relationships for existing callers. File paths remain search starting points; command creation sites, package candidate input sites, and handling of missing preferences remain open questions.

# Command, Preference, and Package Version Interface Proposal

The original record left in the 2023 year was brief. At the time, someone traced downward from an editing action in the piano roll, first ran into tool switching, then asked how commands mapped onto project state, whether the window would remember being displayed independently, and where package information came from. They were adjacent in the same usage path, so they were temporarily listed side by side on one sheet.

That sheet did not say that the four types of objects shared an implementation, nor did it propose replacing any existing entry point. It contained only three candidates: keep the current behavior and add an explanation; add a read-only query layer; or put the window presentation and tool selection into the same editing state. The first candidate was the most conservative, the second was justified as making retrieval easier, and the third existed only because the UI looked continuous. There was no material at the time showing where command groups were created or where registry candidates were brought in.

The old investigation treated `OpenUtau.Core/DocManager.cs` as the place to start looking. This habit came from file hits and nearby object terms, not from a complete call graph. The original record gave it too much weight, as though it could explain commands, preferences, and package versions all the way from here; that part of the assessment later needed to be revised, but the file path itself remains a navigation point.

## The Four Threads Split Apart Later

The addendum to the first review did not add a new service name; instead, it split apart the objects that had been placed side by side. Commands should observe state changes and the prior state after undo; preferences should observe the window presentation across saving, closing, and reopening; package versions should observe candidate selection; and tool mapping should be observed separately for the base mode and pen-tool variants. They can be covered in one review because maintainers encounter them along the same workstation workflow, not because they should share a lifecycle.

This split had a practical counterexample. Someone searching by UI would first see the detached window and current tool, and would easily treat them as one setting; someone searching by object name would first see names near the command or document state, but would not know where tool modes were converted. Both routes could answer half the question, and neither could fill in the reference relationships for the other route. Thus, "UI adjacency" was downgraded back to a search convenience rather than a design basis.

During the review, someone suggested merging window state and tool state. The reason was that the page would only need to read one editing object, and operations would not need to jump among several names. The counterexample was that a change in window presentation does not automatically indicate a change in the current tool enum. If the two were merged, a window issue might require tool state to participate in saving, and a tool issue could also be misdiagnosed as a preference-reading issue. This suggestion did not enter subsequent trials.

One margin note was retained: "First make the reversible surface small." It is not a complete design conclusion; it only defines what this page should try. Commands can examine one execution-and-undo cycle; preferences can examine one save-and-reopen cycle; package versions can examine candidate selection; and tools can examine mode conversion. Any trial that starts taking over legacy writes is no longer a small change within this review sheet.

## File Review for the 2024 Year

The second revision began with the local declarations and nearby names in `OpenUtau.Core/DocManager.cs`. The reviewer used `track`, `ucommand`, `execute`, `ucommandgroup`, `docmanager`, and preference-related terms from the old records to locate the relevant items. The results supported continuing to use this path as a search entry point, but did not support a stronger inference: the review did not reveal the full set of creation paths for command groups, nor the point where package version candidates are brought together.

This overturned an early working hypothesis. At the time, someone thought that because several object names were clustered around the same file, a unified wrapper would be easier to maintain. In light of the review, such a wrapper would likely add forwarding, a new name, and a shared failure path, without adding any confirmed relationships. That hypothesis is explicitly discarded here: file adjacency is not proof of a shared owner.

What is being discarded is not the practice of starting a search with a file, but the claim that "finding the file provides a unified explanation". Maintainers can still start from that path, then check commands, preferences, and candidate versions separately. If a call edge has not yet been found, record the object name and the gap; do not introduce a catch-all service just to make the diagram look complete.

The review also preserved the differing approaches to tracing tools. Tracing from the base mode first reveals the conversion from the mode to the public tool value; tracing from the pen tool first reveals variant selection. Both orders are reasonable, but each covers only part of the picture. The order in which window separation, tool category, and temporary override state are read had not yet been fully established, so the second version did not describe them as a single decision.

## Old proposal retained on this page

> Unified entry point draft: all commands, preferences, and package information first pass through the same service, and the piano roll reads only the editing state returned by that service.

This original passage was not deleted. It was once a candidate under review, and people did in fact use the term "unified entry point" to look back through the old materials. The problem with the draft was not that its name was inadequate, but that it put synchronous document state changes, persisted window settings, and candidate version selection on the same path. Tool mode would then be treated as a preference field, and callers would also have difficulty identifying which object should be responsible for abnormal results.

The old draft had allowed the service to supply a "reasonable" result when a value was missing. That approach is no longer applicable. Having no candidate versions and missing window preferences are not the same kind of null value; failing to find a command creation path is not a null value that a wrapper layer can fill in either. The draft is retained here to explain why the read/write relationships were not later moved into a single overarching entry point.

There was another minor suggestion that was not adopted: add short aliases for all entry points. This would shorten search terms, but would create a second set of interfaces that callers might come to depend on. The existing object names can already be used to locate things, and adding aliases is no more reliable than recording the gaps. This suggestion is also kept on record and is no longer being pursued.

## A limited trial

The trial did not attempt to connect the four categories of objects, only to separate the observation steps. For the command fragment, an existing undoable change was selected: first record the affected document state, then inspect the state after execution, and finally check whether undo returns it to its original state. The focus here is on whether the description documents the action and the undo boundary in the same local context, not on redefining the command lifecycle.

The preferences snippet covers only the piano roll's window presentation. Change the standalone display setting, save, close, and reopen; check whether the window presentation matches the saved value. Tool enumeration, pen tool variants, and temporary modifier keys should not be mixed into this step. Even if they happen to be visible at the same time, they still do not constitute the same field or the same save action.

The package version snippet handles only candidate text that has already reached the entry point. It needs to distinguish selection when there are multiple candidates, the result when no candidates are available, and where responsibility lies when the text cannot be compared. Display order must not be treated as version order. The material available on this page does not answer whether preview versions in the registry participate in selection, so neither retaining nor excluding them has been made mandatory.

The tools snippet records two aspects separately: base modes and pen tool variants. The former answers which tools the current mode exposes, while the latter answers how the choice of pen tool variant affects the current pen tool. The purpose of recording them this way is to prevent "current tool" from being incorrectly documented as a single persisted setting. If the tool value also changes when the window display changes, first save the trigger sequence and the old and new values, then stop expanding the state object.

There are also four explicit stopping points for the trial: if a command action is to be changed from its existing synchronous behavior to waiting for a callback, stop; if window preferences are to be made responsible for tool selection, stop; if version text must be fabricated when there are no candidates, stop; if the base mode and pen tool variant are to be squeezed into the same field to explain the tool mapping, stop. These stopping points apply to new trials and do not retroactively invalidate existing entry points.

## Entry points revisited in 2025

After work on UTA-202 resumed, the issue was still finding the entry points for commands, preferences, and package versions, with one relationship left unconfirmed. It did not introduce any new Architectural Decisions, but only served as a reminder not to erase the gaps in this material. The local check on the card was also narrowly scoped: have readers who were not involved in the changes look things up again by object name and note the pages and links where they get stuck.

The maintainers then restored several source-code spellings to the lookup record verbatim. These were not proposals for new interfaces, nor did they imply that these objects were created by a single manager; their only purpose was to avoid having to translate public names into a different set of informal terms during lookup. This record also prompted us to change the description from "a unified entry point" to "observe each entry point separately".

Work on Piano Roll Editing Tool Mapping later began under UTA-219. That card shares the same workstation entry point as UTA-202, but the two are not the same state-refactoring effort. The former focuses on mode mapping in everyday editing steps, while the latter focuses on looking up commands, preferences, and package versions. Each of the two cards appears once on this page, as navigation for different lines of observation, not as a reason to merge the objects.

The review table also contains a reminder that was added later: "Do not assign an owner to a path first, then work backward from the owner to infer the relationship." It specifically addresses the situation in which `DocManager.cs` has been overinterpreted. The file can still help locate the entry point near the document state; finding it does not prove that it manages the package registry, nor does it show that the command group is necessarily created here. If the current reference establishes only file adjacency, the conclusion should stop at file adjacency as well.

## Current Narrow Approach

The command and persistence entry points retain their existing public shape: UCommand.Execute applies this state change synchronously, UCommandGroup uses NameKey to expose a localized name key, and DocManager exposes the current document entry through Inst; Preferences.Default's DetachPianoRoll is a persisted boolean; PackageManager.GetLatestVersionString selects the highest semantic version from RegistryVersion.version.

This framing is placed after the historical record because it addresses the current entry-point shape, not the polishing of the old draft. It does not establish a central service, nor does it merge the four types of objects into shared state. Commands are still treated as undoable state changes; the window presentation remains part of persisted preferences; version selection is still handled according to semantic versioning; and tool mappings still need to record the base mode and pencil-tool variant separately.

### Command Observation Boundaries

For the current trial, use existing undoable commands rather than create a new command wrapper. Record the affected document state before execution, record the change made this time afterward, then undo it and check whether the previous state returns. If the observation itself exposes more than one creation path, record the path differences first; do not assume that they have the same save timing.

A command-group name should be handled only as a localization name key. Do not concatenate it into window preferences or package entries just to display the name; nor should you add another set of display fields to the command group merely because a creation path has not yet been found. Requirements that would change undo semantics or the synchronization boundary should be made into a separate decision, not hidden in the entry-point explanation.

### Piano Roll Window Observation

Open the piano roll, change the independent display settings, save, close it, and then reopen it. Record whether the display presentation and persisted value remain consistent. Do not inspect the tool category here, or infer the current pencil tool from switching windows. Both are part of the editing experience, but the reasons for reading and saving them differ.

How to handle missing or corrupted preferences, or read anomalies, is still not decided by this page on the caller's behalf. There is not enough local context to determine the order between the default value and the saved value. New adapters must not turn an empty value into an apparently definite tool choice, much less use window state to conceal the read order.

### Package Candidate Observation

The version entry point accepts only candidate text that has already been supplied. During observation, distinguish among the highest semantic version, the absence of usable candidates, and text that cannot be compared. When there are no candidates, retain the existing empty fallback; do not fill in a default version merely to make it easier for the UI to display. Otherwise the caller will lose the distinction between "no available item" and "an item was selected."

The source of package candidates has not been fully confirmed in this material, so this proposal does not lay down a fixed rule for preview versions. If a filtering policy is indeed needed later, a separate proposal should be created that explains the migration cost for existing callers. The current proposal only preserves the existing shape of the selection entry point.

### Recording tool mappings

The tool section continues to record mappings in both directions. For the base modes 5, 6, 7, and 8, the externally exposed tool values are `PitchLineTool`, `PitchSCurveTool`, `PitchSineWaveTool`, and `PitchSmoothenTool`, respectively. These modes belong to the pitch-editing tool category. The pen tool variant is represented by `PenToolVariation`, and it should not be treated as part of window attachment or package version selection.

Set membership checks and pitch checks must also be considered separately. `IsMatch` is used to determine whether the current tool belongs to the given `EditTools` set; `IsPitchTool` is used to determine whether the current mode is a pitch-editing mode. If the temporary override state changes during trial use, record that transition separately rather than documenting it as a basis for an automatic change in tool category.

The goal of tool mapping is not to renumber all editing tools. It only requires maintainers to be able to reconstruct a switch from four perspectives: the base mode, the pen tool variant, the current tool, and the tool category. If these four can only be explained through a single aggregate state, that means the original separation assumptions on this page need to be reviewed again, rather than immediately adding fields.

## When to roll back new changes

What gets rolled back is newly added wrappers, documentation, or trial branches, not existing entry points or historical records. Roll back if a command's synchronous state changes are forced to become asynchronous waits; roll back if undo cannot restore the pre-execution state and the cause is unknown; roll back if the piano roll's saved value does not match its displayed form after reopening; roll back if the package entry point passes off a no-candidate result as version text; roll back if, after the tool mapping is rewritten by the aggregation layer, the tool value is inconsistent with the pitch tool check.

Simply being unable to find a particular caller is not a reason to add an alias or a new service. If command execution, preference storage, or version selection needs to be changed, first explain the migration cost borne by existing callers. The current proposal goes no further than "preserve entry points, add local documentation, and observe separately."

## Related issues still outstanding

1. Whether command group name keys are saved at the same point across different creation paths still needs to be established using actual references.
2. There is currently no directly applicable local rule for which display mode the piano roll chooses when preferences are missing.
3. Whether preview versions in the registry are included when selecting the highest version has not yet been confirmed on this page.
4. When switching tool modes, whether the order in which temporary and persisted state are read changes the observed result needs to be checked again against the actual steps.
5. How `DocManager.cs` directly relates to where commands are created and where package candidates are brought in still needs to be investigated by following the current references.

These questions will affect subsequent plans, but they do not change the limited trial here. In particular, just because maintainers start investigating from the documentation entry point does not mean every subsequent operation should be attributed to the same object.

## Old Meeting Excerpts and Outdated Examples

A note in the meeting margins once read: "Open the piano roll, switch tools, then save preferences; if it is still a separate window next time, that shows the entry point is working correctly." This statement is retained as an early example, but it no longer applies. Another old statement was: "Commands, preferences, and package versions are all near `OpenUtau.Core/DocManager.cs`, so start looking here for all of them." It still explains where the old investigation started, but it cannot explain the reference relationships among the objects. Today, that path can still be used as an entry point, but once the items are found, commands, preferences, and package candidates must be recorded separately.

The old draft for a unified service is also retained: all entry points first go through a single service, which then decides on commands, windows, and package versions. That draft was not included in the current trial. Different lifecycles do not disappear just because the service has a unified facade, which instead makes differences in undo, persistence, and candidate selection harder to trace back.

Confirmed base-mode numbering, correcting the 5-through-8 list above. Base mode 2 is EraserTool and base mode 3 is KnifeTool; neither is a pitch tool. After the user clicked Cancel, the window did not immediately indicate the next step, and there was still CPU activity on the machine. Preserve the UI and model directory from before cancellation; do not click Start, Cancel, or Retry repeatedly in succession. When the window becomes usable again, note whether the result is empty, old, or still waiting; if the window does not recover, stop there.

```text
Tool changes only the highlight: record the current mode and last action; do not change shared computation yet.
Tool changes the editing action too: trace back to where the tool is entered.
Only one direction is known for the spline: leave the input and result, and wait for curve-segment information.
Still waiting after cancellation: preserve the state; do not create a second request.
```

# Troubleshooting Tree for Editing Tools and Transcription Sessions

The draft from 2023 has not been deleted. At the time, piano roll tools, inverse spline queries, and transcription cancellation were put on the same page because operators all said, "I've already done the action, but the next step didn't happen." After review, that shared description can only help us capture the feedback; it does not prove that all three follow the same state path.

## Start with the Editing Behavior

When candidate items display incorrectly, editing actions may still work correctly; when editing actions go wrong, a candidate item may still be highlighted. Early records called both cases "the tool didn't switch," so some people just reopened the window while others went straight to the editing entry point. The descriptions left behind did not line up.

The on-call margin note now says: as long as the user can still perform the original editing action, collect the modes before and after the switch, the selected objects, and the last gesture. Don't change shared computation just because the highlight changed. Only if the minimal editing action has changed should you go back and investigate around the switching action. Neither branch requires the person handling the incident to guess a function name first.

Reopening the piano roll temporarily cleared the highlighting issue a few times. That only shows that the symptom was no longer visible after rebuilding the view. There is no record of whether the original state was passed through correctly, nor any comparison of tool values before and after reopening. This workaround can still help users keep working, but it is no longer evidence that the issue is fixed.

Two names were noted in the margin at the time: `IsMatch` checks whether the current item is among the given candidates, and `IsPitchTool` identifies pitch editing. These names came from a local section of code. There was not enough evidence from the incident to show how their results reached the view, so the names were not written into the procedure.

## The Inverse Spline Question

The spline boundary is narrower than the tool boundary. If someone gets a curve value from a horizontal coordinate, just record the input and output. If they want to get a horizontal coordinate from a curve value, first ask whether that segment is monotonic. Without a record of monotonicity, stop; do not substitute a successful result from another segment.

An early note turned "forward lookup works" into "spline queries are working." That claim was too broad. It is retained here so old feedback does not get copied again unchanged. The inverse-query name was also treated only as an entry point to verify at the time. One successful forward sample cannot establish that the inverse-query conditions have been met.

One review followed `OpenUtau.Core/Editing/LyricBatchEdits.cs` in an attempt to explain tool state, spline queries, and transcription cancellation together. What it found was local code around batch editing operations, not a call relationship connecting all three. The file remains a starting point that can be opened from the old records, but it should not be treated as the sole home of these behaviors. Nor does it establish that transcription sessions originate from the editing entry point.

## Additional Notes on Transcription Cancellation

Start by branching on the state visible to the user:

```text
UI is usable after cancellation
├─ Record the request before cancellation, the model directory, and the visible result
└─ Do not start again immediately; first check whether an old result is already present

UI is still waiting after cancellation
├─ Preserve the window state and CPU activity
├─ Do not change the model directory or click Cancel repeatedly
└─ Wait for a definite return, an error, or a manual abort

A result appears, but the path is questioned
├─ Record the result the user sees
└─ Whether CPU fallback occurred: do not draw a conclusion from the symptoms yet
```

"CPU is still busy" is only an incident signal here. It does not show that the model has been opened or that fallback has completed. The window becoming responsive again also cannot, on its own, show that cancellation happened before the session started. Someone once suggested retrying immediately after cancellation; someone else suggested waiting until CPU finished. Neither suggestion retained the corresponding actual call, so they cannot be listed together as a fixed procedure.

The summer on-call addendum requires more precise cancellation timing: just after the request was submitted, while waiting, or after a visible result had already appeared. The available records still do not contain enough evidence to map those points to internal stages, but recording them can at least keep different incidents from being conflated into a single failure. If the request before cancellation and the user-visible result are missing, leave the report incomplete. Do not invent "fallback completed" or "recovered."

Another mistaken assumption came up in a discussion: since both tools and splines are in the editing UI, an incorrect inverse spline result should lead to checking the piano roll first. That order was not adopted. An inverse curve query depends first on whether the curve segment permits a query in that direction. View state can only be another branch to investigate; it cannot replace the curve conditions.

## Gaps Still to Fill

This page does not yet have numerical examples of its own or a call trace that can describe the transcription session's state changes. The retained action items are:

- [ ] Add the actual path from the tool-switching action to the UI display.
- [ ] Record a minimal input and output for a monotonic spline segment.
- [ ] Find the request, model directory, and user-visible result from one cancellation incident.
- [ ] Distinguish whether a new transcription result had already appeared before or after cancellation.

The old "recovered after reopening" approach can still serve as a temporary workaround. It is not a release criterion and should not override the separate stopping points for tools, splines, and sessions.

# Troubleshooting Tree for Editing Tools and Transcription Sessions

This page was initially tucked into field notes for the piano roll. Later, transcription cancellation and CPU rollback were added as well, for a simple reason: users all said they had performed the action but did not get the expected next step. This wording is useful for handling field reports, but not for defining a single failure. The old paper was never separated, and instead retained traces of several occasions when adjacent symptoms were mistaken for the same chain.

## 2023-06-05: The Original Paper Edge

The earliest reproducible case involved two manifestations after switching tools. In the first, only the candidate item or highlight looked wrong, while the user could still drag, select, or edit as before. In the second, the user only discovered after making a minimal edit that the actual mode did not match the mode they had just selected. At the time, enough before-and-after state was not saved, so reports often called both cases "the tool did not switch."

The temporary procedure at the time was short: switch once, inspect the screen, and then perform one minimal edit. If reopening the piano roll restored the highlight, record it provisionally as residual UI state; if the problem remained after reopening, write down the current mode, selected object, and last operation. This procedure did not answer where the state came from; it only avoided changing shared computation without field evidence.

Only one sentence was left beside the spline: "One direction computes correctly; do not promise the other direction yet." Someone supplied a position and got a curve value, then asked to recover the position from the curve value. The original record did not say whether the curve segment was monotonic, nor did it specify the input and output. The reverse lookup was therefore treated as requiring investigation, and a single forward result was not taken as evidence that the shared capability was already available.

The two lines on transcription were more scattered: after cancellation, the window did not immediately state the result, and the machine still had CPU activity. The operator was asked not to click Start and Cancel repeatedly, and to preserve the model directory and the screen from before cancellation. If the window recovered, record whether the user saw an empty result, a stale result, or a waiting state; if it was still impossible to operate, preserve the situation as is. These are protective steps, not a judgment about the session's internal state.

The old paper used `OpenUtau.Core/Editing/LyricBatchEdits.cs` as a troubleshooting entry point. The only reason was that the issue name and the call name heard at the time both pointed to the vicinity of editor batch operations. This entry point was later retained for historical navigation; it does not mean that the editing tools, shared spline query, and transcription session are in the same file, nor that making changes from here can fix any of the symptoms.

## 2023-06-19: On-Call Margin Notes

"Reopen the piano roll and try again" was written beside several feedback screenshots. It did make some highlighting issues disappear temporarily, but it did not save the mode values before and after reopening, nor did it explain whether the edit action had remained correct before reopening. This practice was therefore treated only as a temporary way to get the user out of the current screen, and cannot serve as evidence of a fix.

Another margin note asks for the actions to be broken down further. First, only switch tools, without dragging any objects; then observe the candidates; finally, perform a minimal edit that does not change too much content. This at least lets us distinguish between "the display has not caught up" and "the editing behavior has actually changed." If switching, dragging, and undoing are done in succession from the start, there is no way to tell which step changed the result during the incident.

The spline record did not ask the operator to try a different point immediately, either. Trying a different point might produce a seemingly normal result, but it would not tell us whether the original curve segment met the conditions for an inverse query. The original input, the returned value, and the direction of the curve segment are more useful than another successful point; this statement was later cited in several pieces of old feedback, but no separate table of examples was created.

## 2023-07-03: Misinterpretations after reopening

Over the summer, people repeatedly used the approach of "reopen the piano roll and try again." Some highlighting issues were no longer visible after reopening, so the old records briefly described this as an effective recovery. Only on later review did it become clear that there were no comparable mode values from before and after reopening, no minimal sample of user actions, and no indication of whether editing actions had remained correct throughout.

The original statement was therefore not deleted; only the margin note was revised: reopening lets the user leave the current view, but does not prove that tool state synchronization succeeded. When only the highlighting is abnormal, save the modes and candidates from before and after the switch, along with the last action; only if the editing action itself also changes should the investigation return to the tool-switching entry point. A single success after reopening must not supersede the original incident evidence.

At the time, someone wanted to combine "whether the candidate tool matches" and "whether pitch editing is currently active" into a single checkbox to make on-call handling easier. This proposal was not carried forward. The two conditions may occur in the same incident, but they are not the same problem; once they are combined into one label, subsequent reports cannot distinguish display abnormalities from editing behavior abnormalities.

This revision also left a small gap. The records only said "current tool," without consistently recording the value before switching, the value after switching, and the action the user actually performed. Later, one person used a screenshot showing only highlighting to prove that editing had failed, while another used a screen recording of a successful edit to prove that there was no problem. The two pieces of evidence did not actually cover the same thing.

## 2023-08-24: Led astray by filenames

The review in month 8 tried to follow the old paths to find a common explanation for three questions: who stores the tool state, who provides spline queries, and whether canceling transcription goes through the editing entry point. The result only identified some relevant files, without establishing a call relationship linking all three.

An overly confident working hypothesis was recorded at the time:

> The entry point near the editing batch operations should be responsible for tool checks; inverse spline queries may just be an internal helper for that entry point; transcription cancellation probably rolls back along the same state path.

This original wording was retained to explain why file locations were no longer used later to assign investigation directions. It had no test cases and no call stack. The last sentence in particular cannot guide session troubleshooting; the superficial similarity between tools and sessions is at most a search clue, not a causal relationship.

The review also exposed an omission. When reporting that "CPU was still working after cancellation", people did not consistently record whether cancellation occurred before or after the model was loaded, nor did they record whether the user had already seen new transcription results. As a result, "still busy", "recovered", and "no results" were used interchangeably across records, making comparison impossible.

This review did not lead to a decision to make changes. It only narrowed the use of the old entry point to "continue looking for local declarations from here" and recorded the tool, spline, and session as three separate objects. If only the issue name and file location are available at the scene, only the symptoms can be retained; the filename cannot be treated as an assignment of responsibilities.

## 2023-08-31: Action tree for cancellation scenarios

The tree left after that review was intended to preserve the state at the scene:

```text
Transcription results did not appear as expected
├─ Still able to interact after cancellation
│  ├─ Record the request before cancellation, the model directory, and the user-visible results
│  └─ Do not start again immediately; first check whether old results remain on the page
├─ Still waiting after cancellation
│  ├─ Preserve the window and CPU activity
│  ├─ Do not change the model directory or click cancel repeatedly
│  └─ Wait for a return, an error, or a manual abort
└─ Results have appeared, but the execution path is in question
   ├─ Save the results the user saw
   └─ Do not infer from CPU activity that fallback has already occurred
```

The tree contains no time value for "how long to wait before retrying". The old records did not provide a reusable duration, nor did they correlate CPU activity with the point when the model session was opened. Adding a wait duration just to make the procedure look complete would turn a guess into a rule.

Here, "still able to interact after cancellation" describes only the window state; it does not mean the session has stopped. "Still waiting" does not mean fallback has started either. Both states require saving the request before cancellation and the user-visible results, because the same CPU activity may occur at different stages. When the request content is unavailable, subsequent handling should only preserve the state at the scene, not replace the old request with a new one.

Two old suggestions remain in the meeting draft. One was to restart immediately after the user cancels, to get new results as quickly as possible; the other was to keep waiting as long as CPU remained busy. Each captured one phenomenon, but neither recorded the stage at which the request was canceled or stated whether old or new results had appeared.

Later, neither suggestion was treated as a default step anymore. When interaction is still possible after cancellation, first save the visible results, then decide whether a new request is needed; when still waiting, do not trigger the operation again, to avoid mixing a second request into the first incident. CPU activity is treated only as an observation that needs to be preserved, not as evidence that "the session has loaded" or "fallback has completed".

## 2023-09-12: Debate over spline direction

The spline section was reviewed separately afterward. A forward lookup only needs to retain the x-coordinate and the resulting curve value; a reverse lookup first asks whether the curve segment is monotonic. Without monotonicity information, stop at the data conditions instead of sending the issue back to the piano-roll display state.

This was a correction, not an additional implementation note. The earlier wording—"the forward calculation works, so the reverse calculation should work too"—is no longer used. The fact that another curve segment happens to produce a usable result cannot make up for the lack of a monotonicity record for the current segment. If more work is needed, first leave the minimum input, output, and segment conditions.

On one occasion, someone on site attributed the reverse-lookup failure to a stale value cached after switching tools. No evidence was retained for this claim: there was neither the state before and after the tool switch nor the curve-segment conditions. It was marked in the margin of the old page, followed by "Check direction and monotonicity first." This does not mean the display is never relevant; it means this record has no basis for treating it as the primary cause first.

This correction also explains why the two objects cannot be combined into a single troubleshooting box. The tool scenario takes selection, candidate items, and the edit action as input; the spline scenario takes position, curve value, and segment-shape conditions as input. Both may be described by users as "not getting the next step," but they require different minimum records.

## 2024-01-18: Meeting excerpt

The later review accepted neither "reopening the window is the fix" nor "the filename can indicate responsibility." The remaining comment was brief: first separate observable tool categories, curve direction, and the cancellation scenario; write the stopping point for each branch; when there is no call or log, do not fill in the story with a familiar module name.

Only after the review was the order on this page fixed. The tool branch asks what the user selected, what the interface displayed, and what the minimum edit action did; the spline branch asks about the input direction and the curve-segment conditions; the cancellation branch asks about the cancellation timing, the model directory, and the user's last visible result. The three sets of records may occur on the same day, but that does not make them a single owner or a single change point.

Someone also proposed that, since `OpenUtau.Core/Editing/LyricBatchEdits.cs` is easy to search for, all related anomalies should first be routed to the editor branch. The proposal did not pass. A path can help open old materials, but it cannot replace call relationships; an issue in a transcription session still needs its own request, cancellation timing, and result records.

Another retained comment was that the page should not promise a complete investigation merely because it has an adjacent entry point. A tool-highlighting anomaly may have no effect on the minimum edit action, a reverse-lookup failure for a spline may simply mean that the segment conditions are not satisfied, and CPU activity after cancellation may not indicate the stage of the model session. Compressing all three into one conclusion would instead erase these differences.

## 2024-04-07: Old procedure draft

The following section once appeared at the end of the old link; it is retained because people still start reading here:

```text
Wrong tool: reopen the piano roll and try again.
Spline does not return: try a different point; if it returns, count it as a pass.
Transcription is not progressing: wait for CPU, then retry.
```

None of these three lines can now be followed directly. The first line does not preserve the state, the second does not check the monotonic segment, and the third may create a second request before cancellation has completed. They reflect the temporary workarounds available at the time, not the basis for assessment added later.

The old procedure draft has not been deleted because it still appears at the end of several old links. Readers who see only these three lines can easily mistake "the user can temporarily continue working" for "the internal state has recovered." So the original text was retained and stop conditions were added after it, rather than rewriting the old approach into new steps that appear correct.

## 2024-06-22: Related items that remain unresolved

Vertical scaling in the track header area was once mentioned alongside tool highlighting. The existing records contain no usable area, heights before and after scaling, or undo process, so this can only be retained as a related issue in the editing interface, not folded into the tool troubleshooting tree. It belongs to the same editing context as the piano roll, but that does not mean it is already within this page's troubleshooting scope.

Another unresolved item is how users can determine which execution path was taken after transcription results appear. For now, only the model directory and user-visible results can be preserved; without the environment, logs, or call snippets, no comparison can be made between CPU and other execution methods.

There is also a minor issue that has not been filed elsewhere: when users see old results after cancellation, the generation time of those old results and the current request were not recorded together. The page may simply still be showing the previous results, or the new results may not yet have replaced them; the existing material is insufficient to choose either explanation. Keep it in the cancellation branch for now, without moving it to the tool or spline sections.

## 2025-02-10: Current position placed toward the end

The old combined assessment ends here. The shared computation interface for the piano roll and splines remains directly queryable: EditTool.IsMatch determines whether the current tool is in the candidate set, and IsPitchTool identifies only pitch tools; CubicSplineSegment.GetY computes y from x, and GetX computes x inversely from y on a monotonic segment.

This position addresses only the boundaries of tool classification and spline queries. It does not explain why highlighting failed to update or whether the session was already open at the time of cancellation, nor does it interpret CPU activity as any particular execution path. The before-and-after states, inputs and outputs, or cancellation timing should still be preserved from the actual occurrence, with investigation continuing along the respective branches.

If the tool value belongs to the candidate set rather than being a pitch tool, record both results instead of forcing them into a single item; if it is a pitch tool but the candidate display is abnormal, likewise leave the display issue in the tool branch. The spline forward result can be recorded as position-to-curve value; verify the reverse result only on monotonic segments. On-site personnel are not required here to infer the entire state flow from a single UI symptom.

The current guidance in this section does not treat transcription cancellation as the same rule set. Cancellation still starts from the state visible to the user: save the request, model directory, and result from before cancellation; do not trigger it again while the window is still waiting; after the window recovers, do not determine that it has rolled back solely from CPU activity. This connects to the previous old tree, but does not erase the misjudgment recorded in that tree at the time.

## Next steps retained at the bottom of the page

The outstanding content has not become a conclusion: a minimal input/output example for a monotonic spline segment; the actual path from tool state switching to display; and the request, model directory, and user result from one cancellation incident. The old entry point can help locate these materials, but this page no longer uses it as a substitute for the actual incident.

If real calls or logs are added later, place them in the corresponding branch rather than going back and rewriting the judgment from 2023 year. The old paragraphs record the phenomena that could be seen at the time; the guidance from 2025 year only narrowed the wording of the public query and did not serve as evidence for the old screenshots, incorrect attributions, or incomplete records.

# Phonemizer Expression and Duration Compatibility Workflow

The migration changes from only comparing phoneme output to first retrieving the expression configuration passed into UTrack, then checking the validation results. Retain the old record; if verification fails, restore from it rather than wrapping the anomaly separately.

```text
Old: only compare phoneme output
New: UTrack expression configuration → validation
Fallback: restore the old record
```

Phonemizer.SetUp must be bound to the expression configuration passed into UTrack: GetParentToneShift and GetParentAlternate return numeric defaults, GetParentVoiceColor selects the VoiceColor option using CustomDefaultValue as the index, and GetParentConsonantStretchRatio derives a ratio from velocity; UPhoneme.Validate must retain the existing ErrorException instance, and Error must continue to be true.

Default remains the preference entry point and cannot serve as this migration's fallback. UTA-204 are reserved for in-situ verification of the default expression; UTA-221 only record what duration accumulation quantization actually returns or throws.

TODO: After restoring the old record, who fills in the final result?

The velocity ratio is fixed, not any monotone function of the custom default. GetParentConsonantStretchRatio returns 2 raised to the power of (1 minus velocity divided by 100), using the track velocity custom default. At the neutral default of 100 the ratio is 1. At a custom default of 75 the ratio is 2 to the power of 0.25, about 1.189. Inverting the exponent is a different ratio and is not this contract. When no track velocity descriptor is present, the ratio is 1.

# DiffSinger Original Script Field Experiment Log

This review still starts from `OpenUtau.Core/DiffSinger/DiffSingerBasePhonemizer.cs`. The path is in `internal/UTAU`'s `v_prev`, and the available content consists of partial field declarations and adjacent navigation; the file location was not directly treated as indicating ownership of the complete implementation. For this round, the record includes only the original script's inputs and outputs; phoneme calculation and render caching are not included.

The samples were split into three facets: lyric or note text, frame duration, and tension curve. The text was examined separately at the key and value level, while the curve kept separate samples for negative values, breathiness, and voicing; time steps were checked using a fixed 10 ms input. This separates "whether the fields changed" from "how the numbers are written out," so locale settings or display formatting in the UI do not mix the two.

The text fragments retained from the actual review are: the negative half-value for tension was `-0.500`, breathiness was `0.125`, and voicing's 0.75 was written as `0.750`. The energy sample `1.250 -2.500` is space-separated; retain the entire segment rather than looking only at the first value. The two time steps corresponding to the 10 ms frame were both written as `0.01`. Time values are recorded in seconds, which is not the same format as the curve samples' three decimal places.

The visible field names for RawDiffSingerScript are fixed: text carries lyric or note text, energy_timestep and tension_timestep are both converted from frameMs milliseconds to seconds, and tension carries the tension curve; field names and meanings must not change with locale settings.

The field order must also be preserved with the full export. Extracting only one curve line cannot show whether the text, time steps, and curve still belong to the same script; a UI preview alone cannot replace the raw text. The observation retained here stops at these outputs and does not extend to how playback position or multitrack state changes them.

# Phoneme Fade Boundary and Variance Serialization Decision

This time, handle Phoneme Overlap Fade Boundaries and DiffSinger Invariant Variance Region Serialization under the same release decision. Both concern "where the change starts being counted"; if each retains its own boundary convention, the same edit result may look inconsistent on the playback and script sides during regression.

The entry point reviewed is `OpenUtau.Core/Ustx/UPhoneme.cs`. The determination here should be anchored in the adjacent-phoneme relationship: the current phoneme has `Next`, and overlap and tail overlap should not be treated as two independent sources of fading. Previously, the length was first determined from the current phoneme's crossfade, then the successor's influence was added; when the overlap nears the boundary, the fade-in and fade-out each take part of the interval, making the result difficult to explain.

Two directions were discussed.

- Retain two calculations: the playback side considers only audible fading, while the script side considers only the unchanged region. The advantage is that the change is small; the drawback is that every boundary sample requires an explanation of why the two can differ.
- Define the boundary using the same adjacent-phoneme relationship, then map it separately to fading and serialization. The advantage is that regression samples can be shared; the drawback is having to accept that script export is also constrained by phoneme adjacency.

The second option was chosen at the time. On the phoneme side, use the current item, `Next`, overlap, and tailOverlap as boundary inputs; the unchanged region of DiffSinger is also extracted according to this result. "No overlap" was deliberately not listed here as a special serialization rule; zero overlap is treated as just one value of the same determination.

This decision also carries an assumption: outside the boundary, the variance curve does not need to retain content that reflects the transitions before and after. If it is later found that the exported curve still needs to be continuous at the seam, revisit this assumption first rather than continuing to add compensation separately to the fade-in and fade-out. Otherwise, this would return to two boundary definitions.

Before release, only two types of samples need to be retained: one where a successor phoneme exists and has overlap, and one where a successor item exists but tail overlap is zero. The former is used to confirm the boundary value; the latter is used to confirm that no fade or variance segment is generated out of nowhere merely because `Next` exists. The specific script fields for the samples have not been added here yet.

The tentative conclusion is: the boundary belongs to the adjacent-phoneme relationship, not to an individual phoneme's local attributes; the region where variance remains unchanged follows that relationship. If the inspection results do not match this, first withdraw the assumption that the same boundary can serve playback and serialization at the same time, then record the two entry points separately.

Playback fade lengths and variance retention are separate contracts; the shared-boundary assumption above is withdrawn. GetFadeIn uses the overlap length only when this phoneme is overlapped and crossfade is enabled; otherwise the fade-in falls back to 5 ms. GetFadeOut uses tailOverlap only when the next phoneme is overlapped and crossfade is enabled; otherwise the fade-out falls back to 35 ms. Variance patches do not follow that phoneme boundary. Changed pitch frames take the new variance and blend symmetrically into unchanged neighbors on both sides. Distant frames keep their old variance values. The exact fade-window length is an implementation choice, not one shared phoneme boundary.

# Playback Splitting and Speaker Suffix Plan

Initially, Voice Part Splitting at the Playhead, phonemizer overrides, and speaker suffixes were written up as a single window-side trial because all three were raised in the piano-roll editing context. At the time, the assumption was that a single operation could record the playback position, component changes, and pronunciation selection together. Later review found no evidence of a shared command or shared persistence layer, so that assumption is no longer a prerequisite for the trial.

The old merged proposal is retained: it explains why the early notes put the two issues together, and shows that the primary concern at the time was that the operation chain was too long, not the object boundary. It cannot, on that basis, imply that a split result affects the override or that suffix input changes the voice component. The current arrangement is to collect the two types of results separately, then decide whether it is worth returning to the same entry point.

UTA-207 serve as the recording entry for the split scenario: both a successful call and a failed call must have a visible result. UTA-224 start from the pre-call state for overrides and suffixes, and require confirmation of whether any additional changes appear after completion. The two cards provide only their respective observation entry points; they have not been combined into a single release action.

## Split Records

First select a voice component that can be located in the piano roll, place the playback position inside the component, and perform one operation. Record the component's displayed name and the playback position before the operation, along with the number of components afterward. If the interface shows two components, any name change can be retained as an observed result, but do not assume that a name suffix is a stable rule. Then move the playback position near the boundary and save the result from this round separately; do not fold it into the internal-position sample.

The boundary sample may have no second component, or the interface may change without making it possible to identify whether the object has actually been split. In the latter case, do not deem the split complete based only on a window refresh. If undo is available, also compare the component count and display state after undo: only when both return to a single component does this count as restoring the original state. If only the display returns while the component count remains different, leave this record as a failure item and do not continue discussing naming or linkage.

The early draft tended to settle the naming handling at the same time. That order is no longer used. First confirm whether two identifiable result components were produced, then check whether the names are retained and whether numbering is needed, avoiding turning display-layer speculation into an interface requirement. The playback position itself is recorded only as an operation condition; this round does not infer its complete relationship to the underlying tick or document state.

## Override and Suffix Records

For the override portion, fix one note and its parent track state, then change only the phonemizer override value. Record the current phonemizer and note text at the start. At the end, check only whether pronunciation processing shows the expected difference and whether the project or interface has left any additional changes. Do not enter a suffix at the same time; otherwise, it will be impossible to distinguish whether the result came from the override or the suffix selection.

The second round starts from an equally clear starting point and changes only the speaker suffix. Keep one record for a configured suffix and one for an unknown suffix. Even if neither produces usable pronunciation, they cannot be collapsed into the same failure: the former may mean the input was accepted but no visible change appeared, while the latter may stop at the input-recognition or diagnostic stage. The record should retain the original suffix input; do not write only "suffix failed."

There is still no conclusion here as to whether the override is persisted independently, nor whether the suffix leaves project-level changes. The old draft treated these as one persistence investigation; they are now listed as two different questions pending confirmation. If neither the override nor the suffix leaves a distinguishable subsequent change, retain that result as-is rather than splicing the two rounds together to manufacture unified behavior.

## Entry Tradeoffs

Option A retains a single window-side context: inspect the playback position, editing state, voice components, name, and tick-adjacent position near `OpenUtau/Views/PianoRollWindow.axaml.cs`. It is suitable for keeping the user's action and the result seen at the time together, and keeps lookup cost low. But the window state may obscure the command boundary; when the result is wrong, it is difficult to distinguish an operation that was not triggered, an object that did not change, and a display that was not updated.

Option B separates the records. For splitting, track only before-and-after differences in playback position and voice components; for overrides and suffixes, track only the pronunciation-selection input and end state. This adds one record and one comparison, but avoids misattributing suffix input to splitting. The current trial favors Option B, but it has not yet become an implementation decision.

Option C retains only window-side code inspection and does not schedule object-level records. This can help locate the editing context, but it cannot replace the visible results of a success, a failure, and an undo. If it ultimately yields only window navigation, keep it as a lookup clue rather than writing it up as a complete call chain.

The withdrawal criteria remain strict: if the split result cannot be identified reliably, or undo cannot restore the original state, do not include names, boundary behavior, or linkage in the release notes. If the override and suffix are still mixed in the same record, the failed input has not been retained, or it is impossible to tell which input caused the additional change, do not plan a combined commit.

Open items: whether a boundary position is a valid split position; whether the override is persisted independently; and whether the speaker suffix causes a project-level change. Address these three first; do not expand the trial scope again on the grounds that "they're all done in the same window."

The earlier note that a name suffix is not a stable rule is withdrawn for a successful split of a part named Verse. Splitting that part at the playhead names the two resulting parts Verse-1 and Verse-2. A part at position 100 with duration 1000, split at tick 500, becomes a 400-tick part and a 600-tick part. Notes that fall in the second part are repositioned relative to that new start.

# Track Scaling and Bypassed EQ Troubleshooting Tree

Log the two phenomena seen in this round separately. One is that the track header area becomes too tall with vertical zoom, and occasionally leaves an unexpected stretch of blank space after zooming out. The other is that track EQ appears to produce no change in some auditions. They appeared in the same stability check, but one first points to view dimensions and the other to audio processing, so they should not be handled with the same recovery action.

The header-area follow-up entry is tentatively recorded as `OpenUtau/ViewModels/TracksViewModel.cs`. At this point, all that is confirmed is that the track view and vertical zoom state are adjacent around here. It is not yet known whether the height limit is stored separately or recalculated together with the window's available area. When an anomaly occurs, retain the screen state before and after zooming: header height, whether the track content area changed in sync, whether the action was zooming in or out, and whether the window was just resized. Writing only "the header got bigger" cannot distinguish an overall display change from the header area losing its boundary on its own.

```text
Abnormal header area height
├─ Content area also changes at the same time
│  └─ First record the window and overall view state
└─ Only the header area changes
   ├─ Continues growing after zooming in
   │  └─ Record the zoom direction before it occurred
   └─ Blank space is not reclaimed after zooming out
      └─ Retain the header-area state after zooming back
```

Do not refresh the view at the start. If the blank space disappears after a refresh, that only shows that the current display can be redrawn; it does not show that the zoom value, available area, or header height has returned to the correct relationship. If a refresh is required to continue, record the observations before and after the refresh separately. Do not record "it looks normal now" as having found the cause.

On the EQ side, first fix the same track and the same input segment. Changing the playback position or segment during an audition, or tweaking a parameter along the way, will mix input differences into the result. For this check, ask only two things: whether the current effect is bypassed, and whether the before-and-after processing being compared comes from the same buffer segment. Not hearing a difference does not mean no processing occurred; likewise, unchanged samples may be exactly the result of the bypass path.

```text
EQ sounds close to the original
├─ Current state is visible
│  ├─ Bypass is confirmed
│  │  └─ Treat unchanged samples as expected behavior
│  └─ Not bypassed
│     └─ Record the configuration and comparison range
└─ Current state is not visible
   └─ Stop at the configuration object; do not use an audition to fill in the conclusion
```

Do not yet classify the header area and EQ as a common failure. The header-area branch needs the height, window, and zoom direction; the EQ branch needs the configuration, bypass state, and before-and-after results from the same buffer segment. Later, add the actual location where the zoom limit is determined, along with a directly observable indicator for EQ bypass.
