# Track Zoom and Bypass EQ Troubleshooting Tree

The track title area's anomaly was initially described as "the zoom value does not roll back." On review, that description is too broad. There are at least two situations in the field: in one, after the title area grows, it appears no longer to be constrained by the available area of the current window; in the other, a height relationship that was previously fine only appears wrong after the window size changes. The two symptoms look similar, but the recovery actions differ, so separate them by trigger order first.

The entry point still starts at `OpenUtau/ViewModels/TracksViewModel.cs`. From there, check downward from the track view state; do not infer from the path itself that all height calculations happen in the same place. For each reproduction, retain only the conditions that can change the assessment: whether the window was just resized, whether the current track count changed, whether the anomaly occurred after zooming in or out, and whether the title and content areas changed together. The track name, audio content, and listening result are not the primary records for this branch; do not mix them in yet.

```text
Title area vertical zoom anomaly
│
├─ Appears on the first zoom-in
│  ├─ Height changes with the window size
│  │  └─ First check the display relationship involving the available area
│  └─ Height does not change with the window size
│     └─ Retain the current height and zoom direction
│
├─ Appears only after consecutive zoom-ins
│  ├─ Recovers after zooming out
│  │  └─ Record the last direction change before the anomaly appeared
│  └─ Does not recover after zooming out
│     └─ Compare whether the title and content areas are still out of sync
│
└─ Becomes visible only after switching tracks
   └─ Retain the states before and after the switch; do not treat it as an upper-limit conclusion
```

If the title and content areas expand or shrink together, enter the overall view-size branch first. When the window has just been resized, a docked area has just changed, or the number of visible tracks has just changed, the apparent title-height difference may come from the redistribution of the entire view. First restore the window to a state close to the one before the anomaly, then perform one zoom operation. If the proportions recover together, record it as related to the overall view state. If the content-area proportion is normal but the title area remains abnormal, switch to the title-area-only branch.

Older records directly interpreted "the blank space remains after zooming out" as meaning that the height value had not rolled back. Retain only the symptom now: after zooming out, the display did not stay in sync with expectations. This may be related to the available area, the title-area calculation, or redraw timing; the blank space alone cannot establish that any particular value failed to update. In particular, when the window has also changed, do not treat one failed rollback as evidence that a fixed upper limit has failed.

When only the title area changes, distinguish where the anomaly appears. Exceeding expectations on the first zoom-in is not the same record as appearing only after consecutive zoom-ins. For the former, retain the current window state; for the latter, retain the last zoom direction before the anomaly appeared. If zooming in is normal and the anomaly appears only after changing the window, record the window change as the trigger. If a height difference or blank space remains after zooming out, record whether the title and content areas became unsynchronized after the rollback. A case that becomes visible only after switching tracks must also be listed separately; the switch may only make an existing state visible and does not mean the switch caused the anomaly.

The first round tried only refreshing the view. Sometimes that made the blank space disappear, so it was temporarily treated as recovered. Treat it as an observation action instead: if the symptom disappears after a refresh, the display state can be rebuilt; if it remains, the current display was not simply masked by a refresh. Neither result shows that the upper-limit determination is correct, and neither can replace recording the zoom direction and window conditions. If further investigation is needed, start from the state before the refresh rather than reasoning backward from the refreshed display.

The equalization issue has also been split up. "No effect" includes at least four situations: processing is already bypassed; the configuration does not stably enter the processing object; processing runs, but the input segment is not suitable for distinguishing it by listening; or the result is overwritten by another stage afterward. The first three can be checked near the current object. The fourth cannot be concluded from this record alone, so do not write it as the default explanation.

Before starting the equalization investigation, fix the same track, the same input segment, and the same configuration. For every comparison, confirm that the before and after results come from the same buffer range. If one side comes from the result of playing the entire passage and the other from a local segment, even an identical listening result cannot support a conclusion of bypass, configuration failure, or skipped processing. Align the comparison objects first, then discuss the result.

```text
Equalized output is identical or similar to the original input
├─ Current bypass state is clear
│  ├─ Bypassed
│  │  └─ Record unchanged samples as the expected path first
│  └─ Not bypassed
│     ├─ Configuration cannot be reproduced reliably
│     │  └─ Fix the configuration source and input, then compare again
│     ├─ Before and after are not from the same buffer range
│     │  └─ Invalidate the old comparison and retake the same range
│     ├─ Samples are exactly identical
│     │  └─ Check whether processing entered the target range
│     └─ Samples differ but sound similar
│        └─ Record a processing difference; do not label it bypassed
└─ Current bypass state is unclear
   └─ Stop at the configuration object; do not guess the state from listening
```

The correction that must be retained here is: an equalization result close to the original sound does not mean bypass. Bypass is an explicit processing state; a result close to the original may come from the input, parameters, comparison method, or listening conditions. Conversely, identical samples before and after processing cannot automatically show that the configuration is ineffective, because bypass should leave the samples unchanged. The troubleshooting table should record the state, whether the configuration is reproducible, the comparison range, and the result separately; none of these should replace another.

If the bypass state is already clear and bypass is the expected behavior, identical output can end this round of audio-result checks; there is no need to add more listening attempts. If processing is expected but the state remains bypassed, retain the configuration object and current state, then check whether the configuration actually entered the processing object. Do not change the input segment to hide a state mismatch; changing the segment can only change the listening result and cannot explain why the current state did not change.

If the system is not bypassed, first separate "samples are exactly identical" from "the listening result is similar." Exactly identical samples are a technical symptom that can be investigated further; check whether the comparison range is the actual processing range. Similar listening is only an observation. If the samples already differ, it should not be categorized as bypass. Mixing the two forces later investigators to infer the state from a subjective description.

The two lines still share only the release window; they do not share a processing chain. The title-area branch produces height, available-area, and zoom-direction records. The equalization branch produces the bypass state, whether the configuration can be reproduced, and the before/after results from the same buffer. If both sides show anomalies in the same round, complete each side's minimal record separately first, then compare the order in which they occurred. Still unconfirmed: whether the title area's final upper limit is determined entirely by the available view area; and which inputs produce sufficiently obvious sample changes after equalization with a valid configuration.

versions.body:
# Track Zoom and EQ Bypass Troubleshooting Tree

This troubleshooting record documents two symptoms often reported during the same stability check: the track header area appears too tall after vertical zooming, and track EQ sounds unchanged in some reproduction attempts. Both have appeared during the current release window, but their starting points differ. For the former, first check the view area, header area, and zoom direction; for the latter, first check the effect state, configuration, and buffer. Do not treat a refresh, a track switch, or a listening test as a shared recovery action just because both issues are visible at the same time.

The header area investigation starts at `OpenUtau/ViewModels/TracksViewModel.cs`. This is close to the track view state, making it a good place to first check the relationship between the post-zoom height and the available view area. On the EQ side, start with the current track's effect state and the results before and after processing. Even if the file paths, UI locations, and occurrence times are close, that is not enough to show that the two lines of investigation share the same root cause.

First capture observations that can be compared. For the header area, you only need to record the relative heights of the header and content areas before and after zooming, the zoom direction, whether the window had just been adjusted, and whether the anomaly appeared only after switching tracks. For EQ, you only need to capture the same track, the same input segment, the current configuration, the bypass state, and whether the before-and-after comparison used the same buffer range. When both issues occur, record whether the display anomaly was seen first or the audio anomaly was heard first, in the order they actually occurred; do not work backward from the result of one to fill in gaps for the other.

If you cannot say whether the header area anomaly appeared after zooming in, zooming out, a window change, or a track switch, stop at the zoom branch for now. If the EQ comparison did not keep the same input segment and the same buffer range fixed, stop at the effect branch for now. Vague statements such as "it looks wrong" or "it sounds no different" can serve as the start of a bug report, but cannot support the technical judgments that follow.

```text
Starting point
├─ Track header area height anomaly is seen first
│  ├─ Content area also becomes taller or shorter
│  │  └─ Go to the overall view size branch
│  └─ Content area does not change by the same proportion
│     └─ Go to the header area zoom limit branch
├─ No obvious change in EQ is heard first
│  ├─ Current bypass state is visible
│  │  └─ Go to the effect state branch
│  └─ Current bypass state is unknown
│     └─ Return to the configuration object, do not evaluate the output yet
└─ Both occur at the same time
   ├─ Each can be reproduced
   │  └─ Record them separately, then compare the trigger order
   └─ One of them cannot be reproduced
      └─ Do not use the other issue's result to fill in the cause
```

## Header area: First determine which part is no longer within its bounds

"The header area is too tall" is not a specific enough result. The first step is not to keep scrolling to zoom, but to check whether the track content area is also changing by a similar proportion. When the header and content areas change together, first suspect that the overall visible area has been redistributed; only when the header area changes on its own should you move to the vertical zoom limit branch. Putting this step first avoids mistakenly recording a symptom caused by a window change as a height problem in the header area itself.

### The content area changes too

When the window has just been resized, the docking area has just changed, or the number of visible tracks has just changed, the header area may look unusually tall simply because the overall view dimensions have been redistributed. In this case, first restore the window to a state similar to the one before the anomaly, then zoom just once. Do not move the window, change the zoom direction, and switch tracks at the same time; even if the display returns to normal, you will not know which action changed the relationship between the displayed areas.

If, after restoring the window, the proportions of the title area and content area recover together, record this as "related to overall view dimensions." This does not mean the zooming branch has been ruled out; it means that the current observed behavior primarily depends on the overall area. If, after the window is restored, the content-area proportion is normal but the title area is still clearly too high, switch to the title-area-only branch. What must be retained here is the relative relationship before and after; there is no need to add unrelated audio content, playback position, or equalizer settings for troubleshooting.

Older records directly described "the blank space is still there after shrinking" as the height value not reverting. This wording has now been narrowed: the blank space is still there, which only indicates that the current display is not synchronized with expectations. The window's available area, the title-area calculation result, and refresh timing may all be involved. Without retaining the window state, the blank space alone cannot determine which state failed to update.

When the overall-dimensions branch is triggered, first check that these three records are complete: whether the window differs before and after the anomaly, whether the title area and content area change together, and whether a single zoom operation can reproduce the proportion difference. If one item is missing, do not continue toward an "upper limit failure" description. The current task is to route the observed behavior to the correct branch, not to attribute it to the implementation without sufficient state.

```text
Title area and content area change simultaneously
├─ Window state just changed
│  ├─ After restoring a roughly matching window, the proportions recover together
│  │  └─ Record as related to overall view dimensions
│  └─ Title area remains abnormal on its own after restoration
│     └─ Switch to the title-area-only branch
├─ Window state unchanged
│  └─ Retain the zoom direction and visible-area state
└─ Unable to determine whether the window changed
   └─ Do not classify the observed behavior as an upper-limit issue
```

### Only the title area changes

When only the title area increases noticeably and the content area does not change similarly, first record which type of operation the anomaly occurred after: it appeared on the first zoom-in; it appeared only after repeated zooming in to a certain state; zooming in was normal but it appeared only after adjusting the window; the abnormal height or blank space remained after zooming out; or it only displayed the original issue after switching tracks. These are not implementation conclusions, but they ensure that the next review does not have to start by guessing from "intermittent."

When it appears on the first zoom-in, the current window state and zoom direction are sufficient as the first field record. When it appears only after repeated zooming in, the last direction change before the anomaly must be recorded; the number of repetitions and the direction are themselves part of the observed behavior and cannot be reduced to "intermittent." When zooming in is normal but the anomaly appears only after changing the window, retain the window change as the trigger condition. When it remains abnormal after zooming out, retain the relationship between the title area and content area after zooming back out. When it only becomes visible after switching tracks, retain the before-and-after states, but do not write the switching action as the cause of the anomaly.

The track-view model uses `Bounds` to represent the available view area and uses it to limit track height after vertical zooming. When checking the title-area upper limit, first keep the available area unchanged, then perform zoom-in and zoom-out separately. If the anomaly appears only after the available area changes, leave it in that branch; do not rewrite the observed behavior as a fixed-height threshold issue. If the available area remains unchanged but repeated zooming can still go beyond expectations, retain the zoom direction and display state immediately before the anomaly occurs, for later follow-up through the track-view state.

This requirement also explains why you cannot capture only the final anomalous frame. The final frame can show that the title area currently looks too high, but it cannot show whether the available area changed earlier, nor whether the issue appeared on the first zoom-in or only after repeated zooming. The troubleshooting record needs the minimum operation sequence, not a larger number of screenshots.

### Shrinking did not immediately restore

If the header area still looks too tall after zooming out, do not immediately restart the UI or repeatedly switch tracks. First compare the content area to see whether it also retains the same height difference. If the content area has the same difference, return to the overall view dimensions branch. If only the header area retains blank space, then check whether switching tracks changes the display state. If it changes after switching, that only indicates that the display state has been rendered again; only if it remains unchanged after switching should you preserve the states before and after zooming and continue rechecking the header area height and available area.

```text
Issue persists after zooming out
├─ Content area also retains the same height difference
│  └─ Return to the overall view dimensions branch
├─ Only the header area retains blank space
│  ├─ State changes after switching tracks
│  │  └─ Record the display change, but do not treat it as evidence of a fix
│  └─ State remains unchanged after switching tracks
│     └─ Preserve the header area height, available area, and zoom direction
└─ Recovers only after zooming in once more
   └─ Mark as direction-dependent, do not substitute refresh results for reproduction
```

In one observed case, the issue appeared to clear after refreshing the view. Refreshing can be used as a temporary observation step, but not as a criterion for recovery. It may have recalculated the display state, or it may merely have redrawn the current screen; this page does not combine these two possibilities into a single conclusion. When recording the result, simply write "The visible symptom disappeared after refreshing" or "The issue is still present after refreshing", not "Refreshing fixed the upper limit".

If recovery occurs only after zooming in once more, do not directly describe that result as the zoom upper limit having been corrected either. It shows, at a minimum, that the displayed result depends on the direction of the operation, but it is still insufficient to determine at which step the height is evaluated. In cases like these, it is especially important to preserve the sequence of zooming out and zooming back in, rather than keeping only the final screen showing recovery.

### Stop conditions for the zoom branch

Stop broadening the investigation in any of the following situations: both the header area and the content area change, but the window state was not preserved; only the final screenshot remains, with no zoom direction; the issue appears as the window changes, but there are no before-and-after states; zooming is judged to be correct solely based on the result after switching tracks; or the window, zoom direction, and track selection were all changed during a single reproduction attempt. Stopping does not mean closing the issue, but that the current records are insufficient to support a deeper assessment.

There is still one unconfirmed point in Track Header Vertical Zoom Limit. That point requires event records of inputs and outputs, rather than adding in speculation about EQ, waveform rendering, or the track content area. UTA-208 can be used to navigate to this maintenance entry; the card already has records of reproduction and handoffs from review, and the unconfirmed observed case should remain unconfirmed.

## EQ: first confirm whether processing should currently take place

First reframe "EQ makes no difference to the sound" as a checkable question: whether the current effect is bypassed; if it is not bypassed, whether it has already received a valid configuration and processed the buffer range being compared. Bypass is not a failure result. The bypass path is expected to leave samples unchanged, so identical samples before and after processing do not by themselves prove that the configuration was not received, nor do they by themselves prove that the filter has failed.

Before starting listening tests or comparisons, keep the same track, the same input segment, the same set of configurations, and the same buffer range fixed. If you change the playback position or segment each time, input differences will get mixed into the results; if the before-and-after data are not from the same range, even a similar overall listening impression does not make them comparable. Align the comparison targets first, then assess the state and output.

BiquadEQ reports through `IsBypassed` whether the current configuration will bypass processing and leave the audio samples unchanged. Read this state first, rather than inferring it from what you hear. Listening is especially unsuitable for determining bypass status when the input itself changes very little, the clip is too short, or processing differences are hard to hear.

```text
Equalized output is identical or close to the original input
├─ IsBypassed is true
│  ├─ Bypass is currently expected
│  │  └─ Unchanged samples are normal, end this round of output troubleshooting
│  └─ Processing is currently expected
│     └─ Check why the configuration still keeps the effect processor bypassed
├─ IsBypassed is false
│  ├─ Configuration source is unknown or not reproducible
│  │  └─ Hold the configuration and input fixed first, without evaluating the processing results
│  ├─ The before-and-after comparison does not use the same buffer region
│  │  └─ Discard the old comparison, capture the same region again
│  ├─ Samples are completely identical
│  │  └─ Check whether processing reached the target region
│  └─ Samples differ but sound similar
│     └─ Record this as a processing difference, not as bypass
└─ IsBypassed cannot be obtained
   └─ Stop at state verification, do not use a listening test to fill in the conclusion
```

### Bypass is true

If `IsBypassed` is true, the first question is "is this configuration supposed to bypass processing", not "why can't I hear an effect". If bypass is currently expected, unchanged samples are normal, and this round of output troubleshooting can stop here. If the operator explicitly wants to use equalization but the current state remains bypassed, retain the configuration object and bypass state, and check whether the configuration actually reached the processing object. Do not switch to another audio clip to mask the state inconsistency.

BiquadEQ applies filter parameters through `Configure`, and processes audio after a valid configuration rather than remaining bypassed. If it remains bypassed after configuration, this page only requires recording the states before and after configuration. This alone does not establish that the parameters are corrupted, the filter has failed, or the audio chain was never called at all; those conclusions require different evidence from the affected environment. The wording in older issue reports that describes "bypass" as "the processor was not working" can still help identify the symptom, but is no longer used as a basis for judgment. Bypass, whether configuration was attempted, whether the configuration is valid, and when processing begins are separate questions.

Bypass being true does not require an immediate state reset either. If the goal of the current reproduction is specifically to verify the bypass path, resetting would discard the state that needs to be observed. Treat a reset as a boundary between two observations only when you are ready to start a new round and have finished recording the current bypass state.

### Bypass is false, but the output still sounds like the original

When `IsBypassed` is false, first confirm that the configuration can be reproduced consistently from its source, then confirm that the before-and-after data being compared comes from the same buffer region. When the configuration source is not fixed, alternating changes in bypass state and perceived sound must not be described as random; a different configuration may simply have been used each time. When the input or region is not held fixed, a single instance of identical samples also cannot be attributed to the processing entry point.

Here, "the samples are identical" and "they sound similar" must be kept separate. The former is a clear technical finding: only when the configuration is reproducible, bypass is off, and the comparison ranges are the same is it worth continuing to check whether processing was applied to the target range. The latter is only an observation: if the samples already differ, even if they sound similar, record this as a processing difference rather than reclassifying it as bypass. This keeps subjective listening impressions out of state assessment.

Once configured, BiquadEQ uses `Process` to process audio in place within the specified buffer range, leaving the samples unchanged when bypassed. The key check is therefore whether the comparison range is the target processing range. If you only have results for the entire audio segment but do not know which range was processed, obtain the missing range information first; do not skip this branch just because the entire segment sounds unchanged during playback. When the before-and-after data comes from different ranges, explicitly invalidate the old comparison rather than continuing to add listening records to it.

If the samples are identical, first recheck whether processing was applied to the target buffer range. This is not the same as concluding that `Process` did not execute: it merely puts the relationship between the ranges first under the currently observable conditions. If the samples differ but sound similar, retain the differences and input conditions; there is no need to change clips or expand the scope of the issue just to obtain an obvious audible result.

### Handling repeated configuration changes

When the bypass state or perceived sound alternates across repeated operations, record separately for each operation whether the configuration, state, and input remained the same. If any one of these is not held constant, the results cannot be described as unstable processing behavior. The most common mistake is to hear a difference between two listening tests and immediately attribute it to the effect; when the items being compared have changed, there is not enough evidence for that attribution.

The `Reset` of BiquadEQ clears the filter's runtime state so that subsequent configuration and processing start from a clean state. When you need to restart the comparison, use it as a state operation between two observations: finish the current record, reset, apply the same configuration, and finally compare only one fixed input segment. Resetting does not replace checking the configuration, nor does it mean that the results before the reset were necessarily wrong; it simply prevents the previous runtime state from carrying over into the next round.

Stop following the EQ branch in the following cases: the current bypass state is unknown; the input clip or track was changed within the same comparison round; the configuration object was not retained; only "I can't hear a difference" was recorded, with no sample or range information; the before-and-after data comes from different buffer ranges; or explaining the results requires relying on the unconfirmed state of other effects. These stopping points allow the next attempt to proceed from a clearly defined state, rather than turning a vague listening description into a conclusion.

UTA-225 are used to navigate reliably reproducible issues with bypassable EQ. User paths not yet covered should still be documented on that card. The card can indicate where to start in the field, but it does not replace the branching decisions here about bypass, configuration, and processing ranges.

## When the two lines of investigation can converge again

Only when the title-area and EQ issues can each be reproduced should you compare whether they share the same trigger timing. The facts that can be compared are narrower: whether the title-area anomaly always appears after a particular display-state change, and whether the EQ bypass state also changes during the same sequence of operations. Even if the order is the same, first record this as a correlated observation rather than directly declaring a common root cause.

If the title area issue can be reproduced, while the EQ issue can only be described in terms of how it sounds, complete the title area record first. Conversely, if the EQ bypass state and processing range can be held fixed, while the title area only occasionally looks too tall, complete the EQ record first. Each line of investigation has its own stopping conditions, and they do not need to be closed out together in the same round. Forcing the two into a single fault will make even the usable partial states meaningless.

For the current recheck, start the title area investigation with the track view state of `OpenUtau/ViewModels/TracksViewModel.cs`, and check how the height after vertical zooming relates to the available view area; for EQ, first obtain `IsBypassed`, then check the state after `Configure` and the buffer range compared by `Process`. DOC-22 cover clamping pasted curve values, undo, and compatibility checks for the DiffSinger variance patch. Only turn to that review once the EQ results have ruled out bypass and processing-range issues and the situation actually involves that set of objects; do not treat it as the default follow-up for abnormal track title area height.

Additional stopping condition: if reproduction results for the same track differ before and after bypass, retain the input buffer, zoom value, and effect instance identity; when these three are not aligned, do not attribute waveform differences to EQ parameters or expand the investigation to adjacent tracks.

# Curve Undo and Variance Patch Compatibility Workflow

This verification has two tracks. Do not treat curve editing and the DiffSinger variance patch as a single call chain.

For curves, move away from the old investigation entry point first. Previously, an issue name or call name would usually lead to `OpenUtau.Core/Ustx/UCurve.cs`, followed by a search for declarations near `ucurve` and `uexpressiondescriptor`. Compatibility should now be checked through repository regression tests: paste a segment of an expression curve directly, check the user-visible result after clamping, then undo and confirm that the curve returns to its state before the paste. Regression assertions should check results, not whether a particular internal helper function was called. With this change, files remain entry points for investigation, while regression tests become the basis for judging compatibility.

Procedure:

1. First save a copy of the curve's state before the paste, and record the paste region and out-of-range points; do not modify the original sample first.
2. Paste within the same editing session, inspect the clamped curve, and confirm that out-of-range values do not carry through to the displayed result.
3. Undo immediately afterward, and compare the curve, selection, and subsequent editing state. Any clamped result remaining after undo counts as a failure of this regression test.
4. Record the failure symptoms together with the regression entry point, then return to `UCurve.cs` to inspect nearby declarations; do not settle implementation ownership prematurely just because the entry-point filename is the same.

For the variance patch, move from the usage described on the help page to verification in an actual directory. First use the existing help page to find the call entry point, then run it once in a directory with no preset state. The check here is whether the cache can handle the rendering state after the patch is merged; do not substitute the clamped curve-paste result for this check. Leave the directory as it is for the first run, and only rerun with the same input on the second run, to distinguish "creating the cache for the first time" from "reading an existing cache." If the call cannot complete in an empty directory, record the step where it stops and return to the help-page entry point. Do not keep guessing about the variance patch implementation based on UCurve.cs.

Keep the old paths for both migrations: while the new regression tests or empty-directory checks are not yet stable, issue names, call names, and `OpenUtau.Core/Ustx/UCurve.cs` can still be used for manual tracing. But the old paths only help locate things; they cannot replace checks of user-visible results or cache behavior.

Compatibility checks must also retain the values before execution, after undo, and after redo for the same operation. If any of these is missing, do not mark that path as closed.

# Package Version and Phoneme Timing Proposal

This round puts package version selection and clearing phoneme timing overrides in one proposal, but they are separate implementation tracks. The former handles multiple version strings in the registry; the latter handles whether the original state can be restored after an edit clears the overrides.

There are two tentative directions for package versions: continue comparing strings in text order and add exceptions for special formats as they come up; or first extract comparable semantic components, then select the higher version from the valid candidates. The former requires fewer changes; the latter keeps the rules more centralized. Handling of invalid strings, missing strings, and equal versions is still undecided.

Clearing phoneme timing overrides cannot mean "set to zero." Before execution, save whether each override exists and its value. During execution, clear the attack and release overrides; on undo, write back the original state. No override and a zero-valued override are not the same input.

# Package Version and Phoneme Timing Proposal

The first draft framed both issues as one interface change. After review, they were split into two proposal tracks. Package versions concern a candidate set; clearing phoneme overrides concerns object state before and after a command. They can be reviewed together, but cannot share inputs, failure symptoms, or rollback actions.

For package versions, both text sorting and parsed sorting remain options. Text sorting leaves the read path almost untouched, but version component counts, prerelease markers, and missing fields will keep requiring extra checks. Parsed sorting first takes the version strings from registry entries, extracts comparable semantic components, and then selects a result from the candidates that parse successfully.

A parse failure cannot simply be treated as the lowest version. An invalid string should not displace a valid candidate because its raw characters sort higher. Missing strings cannot automatically be grouped with malformed strings either: one means no value was provided, and the other means an unreadable value was provided. An empty registry and a registry where every entry is unusable also need to be observed separately. For equal valid versions, do not add sorting by name or input position yet, unless an existing stable order can be confirmed from the existing path.

Experiments cannot retain only the final version. Keep the original candidates and their order, the candidates that actually participated in comparison, and the final candidate or empty result. This is needed to distinguish whether a result changed because of parsing, filtering, or tie handling. During migration, retain the registry's original strings; do not change the values first to hide differences between the old and new behavior.

The phoneme track is narrowed to an undoable command. Before execution, save each override's presence and value. During execution, clear the attack and release overrides; on undo, restore the snapshot. Fields that originally had no override cannot be represented by zero, or undo will create a new zero-valued override.

Redo needs its own investigation. After the first clear, the object no longer carries the original overrides; rereading the object during redo would only return the cleared state. Whether the command or the undo group state should hold the snapshot is still undecided. The sequence of clear, undo, and redo must be exercised.

Record timing experiments for four classes of objects: attack override only, release override only, both present, and neither present. For each class, save the presence and value before execution, after clearing, and after undo, and check that the command has not also recalculated neighboring phonemes.

The two tracks have separate rollback conditions: if version sorting produces an unexplained change in valid candidate order, retain the original input and roll back the change; if phoneme undo loses an original override or writes a zero-valued override to an object with no override, stop integrating it into the editing path. `OpenUtau.Core/Format/Wave.cs` is still only a starting point for tracing back; the actual references for the package registry and editing commands must be confirmed individually.

# Package Version and Phoneme Timing Proposal

The earliest record began with a path related to `wave`. At the time, files near the entry point were treated as the implementation locations for the two issues, and package version selection and phoneme override restoration were described as a single interface change. After review, both judgments were withdrawn. `OpenUtau.Core/Format/Wave.cs` can still serve as a starting point for tracing back, but it is no longer used to determine where the implementation resides; follow-up investigation needs to trace references to registry reads and edit commands separately.

There was also an early misunderstanding about the clearing approach: as long as the action was included in an undo group, restoration would follow automatically. The counterexample is that an undo group can only delimit an editing action; it cannot save the pre-execution envelope overrides on behalf of the command. Once execution clears the fields, reading values from the current object during undo will not recover the original state, because it no longer exists. The two approaches remain in the same proposal because they share a review window, not because they share a state model.

For package versions, first try semantic comparison after parsing, rather than continuing to pile exceptions onto text sorting. Version text in the registry is first parsed into comparable components, and selection takes place among usable candidates. This approach does not attempt to define every historical format at once; it only separates character order from version order. If text rules continue to handle changes in the number of version digits, prerelease markers, and missing fields, each subsequent format may require maintainers to add another special case; the parsing path at least concentrates the differences at a single selection entry point.

One boundary must be preserved here: entries that fail to parse cannot participate in a highest-version selection presented as valid, but how failures will be represented has not yet been decided. An entry could be skipped with a diagnostic recorded, or the caller could receive a distinguishable result; the current material is insufficient to combine these two approaches. Missing version text likewise cannot simply be treated as a format error. Trial output must preserve these two original states, rather than leaving only "no version".

Text sorting will not be removed outright in this round. It serves as the comparison path when rolling back, with the advantages of a narrow read scope and the ability to compare existing candidate lists directly; the cost is that every new version format may require another explanation of why character order still holds. Migrating to parsed sorting has a different cost: existing registries may produce a different candidate order under the new rules. If callers depend on that order, the change must be visible in the observations, rather than comparing only the text ultimately returned.

The package version trial retains three layers of results:

1. The original candidates received by the registry and their original order;
2. The candidates that parsed successfully and actually participated in comparison, along with their order;
3. The candidate ultimately selected, or an empty result if no candidate is selectable.

The third layer alone is not enough to explain a regression. A change in the final value could result from different parsing rules, an excluded candidate, or a change in how tied candidates are handled. An empty registry, a set in which all candidates are unusable, and a set containing both valid and invalid text should be recorded as distinct inputs, not all reduced to "no version". If a candidate is missing text, record that absence; if text exists but cannot be parsed, record the original text and the failure status; the two kinds of samples must not be collapsed into the same null value.

No new rules will be added for ties between identical valid versions for now. Without existing evidence, sorting by name or list position would introduce previously unspecified secondary semantics. If the existing read path already preserves a stable order, it can be retained in the trial results with the original input documented; otherwise, leave ties unresolved. Temporarily choosing a secondary key just to obtain stable output would make it difficult during rollback to determine whether a change came from the primary comparison or the newly added tie-breaking rule.

The rollback conditions for the version approach are narrowed to two cases: parsing produces an unexplained change in the order of valid candidates, or a previously usable candidate is excluded and the parsing result cannot explain why. If either occurs, preserve the registry's original input and roll back the parsing change. An empty result must not be presented as a successful selection, nor may the original registry be modified during migration to eliminate differences between the old and new outputs. Whether diagnostics are directly visible to the caller Fang Ke will be decided after the call relationships are confirmed.

On the phoneme timing side, the recommendation is to implement "clear overrides" as an undoable command, without recalculating phoneme durations after clearing. Capture the target phoneme's envelope override state before executing the command, clear the attack- and release-related overrides during execution, and restore from the snapshot during undo. The saved content must include at least whether each override exists and its corresponding value; saving values alone is insufficient to distinguish an empty state from a zero-valued override.

This distinction affects the next edit. If a field that originally had no override is written as zero during undo, it becomes a new override. For input with only a release override, undo must not also create an attack override; the same applies when only an attack override exists. When both exist, each must be restored separately; when neither exists, there should still be no overrides after undo. The restoration target is the same phoneme object that existed before execution; historical state must not be guessed from an object with the same name in the current list.

Redo is a separate branch. The first execution has already cleared the overrides. If redo reads the snapshot from the object again, it will read the cleared result rather than the values from before the first execution. What remains undecided is whether the snapshot is held by the command instance or by the undo group state. A single execution cannot establish that these two storage locations are equivalent; repeated clearing, undo, and redo must be observed to see whether the snapshot still points to the original state. If the object is retrieved again after undo, it is also necessary to confirm that the fields of the same edited object are being restored, rather than creating another override that merely looks identical.

The timing trial records three points for the same phoneme: before execution, after clearing, and after undo; it then adds the state after redo. Inputs must be divided into at least four categories: an attack override exists, a release override exists, both exist, and neither exists. For each category, check whether the overrides are cleared, whether their presence after undo returns to the original state, whether their values return to the original values, and whether redo produces the cleared state again. Testing only a single button click cannot cover these four categories; if the test entry point cannot construct one of them, retain that gap rather than substituting a default object.

Adjacent phonemes are observed only as a boundary check. The clearing target is the current phoneme's timing overrides, not recalculation of the entire chain of adjacent phonemes or replacement of the fade-in and fade-out calculations at the same time. It is necessary to confirm that references to adjacent objects remain unchanged after command execution and undo, and that the snapshot is not written back to a same-named object substituted later. If the fading behavior of adjacent phonemes changes, record it separately rather than treating it as part of the scope already covered by the clearing command.

The comparison of candidates retained in this round is as follows:

| Object | Candidate | Current assessment |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Package versions | Text sorting with exceptions | Small change, but exceptions will increase with the number of version formats |
| Package versions | Semantic comparison after parsing | Trial approach; invalid entries and order differences need to be observed |
| Phoneme overrides | Record only the clearing action | Cannot restore the original values or the state of having no overrides |
| Phoneme overrides | Command saves a pre-execution snapshot | Trial approach; the snapshot's storage location still needs to be determined |

The two trials should not borrow each other's rollback mechanisms. Package version rollback depends on preserving the original candidates and the old selection result, and reloading the project is not a substitute; phoneme command rollback depends on the pre-undo snapshot, and refreshing the project is not a substitute. Bundling both into a single broad change would make it impossible, in the event of failure, to distinguish whether candidate filtering, version comparison, field clearing, or the restoration stage changed the result.

During migration, version text is preserved as-is, and sorting differences are also recorded as-is. Initially, the phoneme command is limited to clearing timing overrides themselves, without also bringing in adjacent phonemes, track state, or package version refreshes. # Offset Components and Effect Notification Troubleshooting Tree

Treat the symptoms as two cases: adding a note in a voice component with an offset, then seeing a result different from before the addition when rolling back; and, after changing a track effect, receiving the change on an object that does not appear to be the track just modified. They were once put on the same troubleshooting path because the earliest entry point was `OpenUtau.Core/Editing/NoteBatchEdits.cs`; new notes, component position, and note duration can all be examined from here.

The old record said, "Just follow the add command first." That was still useful for the first symptom, but too broad for effect notifications. It is kept here to explain why the investigation initially went through the wrong entry point.

## Add Then Roll Back

First record the component offset, the note durations, and the note counts before and after the operation. The position shown in the piano roll cannot by itself be treated as the result; in an offset component, the displayed position and the position within the component may not be the same quantity.

- If the position has already deviated from expectations when the addition completes, stop at the add action and verify that the note entered the expected component. Do not use the later rollback result to explain the position yet.
- If the addition looks normal and the difference appears only after rollback, record separately whether the remaining residue is a note, duration, or position. The three types of residue correspond to different checkpoints and cannot be combined as "undo failed."
- If the undo group contains other edits, split it into one addition and one rollback, then check again. The old record did not confirm the recovery order under consecutive operations.
- If a single operation cannot reproduce the issue, record the offset at the time and whether adjacent notes changed together; "not reproduced" does not mean this path has returned to normal.

Previously, a visible created note was treated as evidence that the rollback chain was working; that is no longer used. The creation result only shows that the add action reached a visible state and cannot replace the post-restoration check.

## Wrong Object After an Effect Change

First distinguish the track whose effect was just modified from the object actually receiving the notification. Do not substitute the currently selected track for the identity in the notification; changing the selection can mask a routing issue.

- If the two are the same, record whether the effect change occurred before or after the selection-state switch, then check for duplicate delivery. Duplicate notifications and an identity error are not the same thing.
- If the two differ, retain the affected track number, the receive order, and the point at which the selection state switched, then stop near message dispatch. Do not return to the add-note branch and force a common cause.
- If no notification was received at all, first confirm that the effect change occurred. If the change did not occur, identity routing cannot yet be determined.
- If this appears only after switching tracks, retain the two track objects from before and after the switch; the old notes did not prove that notification consumers automatically change with the current selection.

Still open: whether linked changes in adjacent notes can alter the restoration result when an offset value and consecutive rollbacks occur together; the consumer entry point for effect notifications has also not yet been filled in from this old investigation path.

# Decision on Separate Modifier-Key States for Notes

During the early investigation, additional visible changes persisted after note editing ended. These were tentatively attributed to incomplete cleanup of modifier-key transitions. At this stage, we will not create separate editing states for Ctrl, Alt, and key combinations; they are treated as conditions attached to the same editing gesture and cleared by a single exit handler when editing ends.

Two approaches were actually compared at the time. The first was to keep the combined check: remember the modifier conditions when editing starts, then discard them together when dragging, marquee selection, or pen-tool use ends. This keeps the state model small and lets the investigation work backward from the end action without first splitting out every key combination.

The other approach was to track modifier keys separately and handle key combinations as distinct input cases. This approach was not shown to be infeasible; there was simply no counterexample at the time showing that a modifier key could affect the result independently of the editing action. Splitting them out immediately would make mouse leave, tool switching, edit cancellation, and window focus loss all cleanup exits that needed checking, with no way during the investigation to tell which one was the source of the anomaly.

Decision: Keep the combined check for this round; do not add separate state transitions. Start the review with the state entry points near `OpenUtau/Views/NoteEditStates.cs` and check whether visible changes still remain after editing ends.

Open questions: When one key in a combination is released first, does it use the same exit handler as releasing all keys? Does canceling an edit also clear the same set of conditions?

versions.body:
# Decision on Independent Modifier-Key States in Note Editing

This record initially treated modifier keys in note editing as a temporary condition of an editing gesture. What was observed at the time was that, after an editing action was completed, the UI still showed changes that should not have remained, so the issue was attributed to an omission in exit handling. On that basis, the initial draft chose not to separate the states: capture a set of conditions when editing begins and clear them all when it ends; it did not require recording the press and release sequences for Ctrl, Alt, or key combinations step by step.

The old decision has not been deleted because subsequent investigations repeatedly looked for the cause in "end actions." It explains why troubleshooting focused on what happened after dragging, marquee selection, and exiting the pen tool, and why the state model was not immediately expanded at the time. However, the initial draft directly turned an observed symptom into a judgment about state structure: something remaining after an operation ends does not mean that all modifier keys are merely one set of conditions that can be merged.

## Trade-offs in the Initial Draft

The first option on the table at the time was to treat modifier keys as supplementary information about whether editing was still in progress. This option had a clear assumption: regardless of which modifier keys the user used, once the same editing session ended, all related conditions should become invalid together. For troubleshooting the reported issue, this assumption had a practical benefit—only two things needed to be checked: whether editing had ended and whether any additional visible changes remained afterward.

The initial draft chose this option not because all input paths had been examined, but because the anomaly had only been reported after the action was completed. No continuous record was kept of pressing a key, establishing a combination, releasing one of the keys first, and releasing all keys. Without those segments, keeping the issue within end handling was a workable provisional judgment.

The other option was to separate individual keys and key combinations into independently observable local states. The initial draft set it aside mainly because of maintenance costs: once separated, the mouse leaving the editing area, canceling an edit, switching tools, and the window losing focus could all become distinct cleanup exit points. At the time, it was not yet possible to say whether these exit points would actually encounter different states, so they were not written up as new implementation requirements.

The phrase "keep the combined check; do not add independent state transitions" in the old document referred to this trade-off. It was a provisional conclusion intended to narrow the investigation at the time, not proof of how state should be stored. Later use of this sentence as evidence that "modifier keys should never have been separated" went beyond the material available to the initial draft.

## Counterexamples Found During Review

Returning to `OpenUtau/Views/NoteEditStates.cs` revealed a direct counterexample to the combined check. The local state was not a generic modifier-key flag; instead, there were three distinct names: `ctrlHeld`, `altHeld`, and `altShiftHeld`. They store the states of Ctrl, Alt, and Alt+Shift, respectively; at least within this object, individual-key and combination states were not collapsed into a single "modifier key present" boolean.

This changes the premise of the old decision; it does not fully explain the entire editing input system. The existence of separate fields shows that the earlier claim that "there is no need to store them independently" was too broad; however, the local state around this file alone still does not establish that every editing tool writes, reads, or clears these values in the same order. The previous record did not collect a complete call chain or retrace every mouse action individually.

In particular, `altShiftHeld` cannot be reconstructed from an abstract "a modifier key is currently active." It preserves the combination relationship. If only a master switch is checked after editing ends, the sequence of holding Alt, then pressing Shift, and then releasing Shift first is collapsed into the same description of ended or not ended, leaving no way to determine when the combination state changed in the reported case.

`ctrlHeld` cannot be treated as an alias for Alt either. When early troubleshooting notes said "modifier key stuck," they did not specify which local state was actually involved; such records could neither distinguish Ctrl from Alt nor reveal whether a key combination was involved. They could only show that the display after editing differed from expectations, not whether the lingering effect was in the input state, the tool result, or the handoff between the two.

## Correction to the Old Conclusion

"All modifier keys share one editing state" is no longer accepted as a description of the local state. When reviewing lingering effects in note editing, `ctrlHeld`, `altHeld`, and `altShiftHeld` should be examined separately, with the timing of their changes recorded. Whether editing has ended is still worth checking, but it can no longer be used as evidence that these states have been merged.

The scope of this correction is narrow. It applies only to the local note-editing state containing `NoteEditStates.cs`, preventing subsequent investigations from rewriting the existing distinctions as a check for any modifier key. It does not decide that all modifier keys should be permanently spread across more objects, nor does it require every read site to consider all three fields at once.

If a behavior depends only on Ctrl, first confirm that it observes `ctrlHeld`; if a behavior depends on the Alt+Shift combination, preserve the information represented by `altShiftHeld` rather than inferring the combination state from the fact that an edit has ended. Changes to Alt alone should be checked against `altHeld`. This decision concerns the granularity of records and judgments, not authorization for a complete rewrite of input logic.

The initial draft worried that separating the states would give each exit point its own reset logic. That concern has not been proven entirely wrong, but it is a maintenance concern rather than an observed behavioral fact. The available material does not answer whether end handling, cancellation handling, and focus-loss handling share a cleanup location; concern about having more exit points is not a reason to treat existing local fields as things that should not exist.

The old decision therefore retains its historical purpose: it records why end actions were checked first at the time and why the input state machine was not immediately explored in the investigation. However, the old decision is no longer a basis for adding editing logic. When this area needs to be changed, first list the fields being observed and their input, read, and clear locations, then discuss which exit points can be merged.

## Moments to Distinguish During Review

The early anomaly was described only as "there are still changes after editing," which places the observation too late. Subsequent records should first state whether the symptom occurs when a modifier key is pressed, a combination is established, one key is released, editing ends, or editing is canceled. Only by recording the timing can we know whether to look back at local state or at the result produced by the tool.

Switching tools during editing is a branch for which no observations have yet been collected. There is currently no conclusion on whether the existing modifier-key state immediately affects the new tool. It cannot be assigned to end handling, nor can it be used to assert that switching tools resets any particular field; this branch needs to be recorded separately from a normal end action.

Canceling an edit must not be conflated with completing an edit either. The initial draft envisioned both as exit handling but did not observe whether they actually pass through the same cleanup location. If the anomaly occurs after cancellation, the record must at least preserve whether Ctrl, Alt, or Alt+Shift was involved at the time and whether the state had already changed before cancellation.

What happens when the window regains focus after losing it is likewise unconfirmed. The existing records contain no material supporting either possibility: that the combination state resynchronizes with the actual key state, or that it retains its previous value. No cleanup sequence is invented here; recording this as a branch to investigate is more useful than continuing to use the old assumption of unified exit handling.

The diagram below only shows which editing stages symptoms should be assigned to during investigation; it does not indicate that these stages already correspond to different implementation paths:

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Editing
    state "Editing in progress" as Editing
    state "Editing finished" as Finished
    state "Editing canceled" as Cancelled
    state "Tool switch" as ToolChanged
    state "Window focus lost" as FocusLost
    Editing --> Finished : Finish editing
    Editing --> Cancelled : Cancel editing
    Editing --> ToolChanged : Switch tools
    Editing --> FocusLost : Lose focus
```

The four destinations in the diagram come from the exit points that the initial draft worried would broaden the investigation. They do not fill in the actual call relationships. At present, the only confirmed fact is that the local fields are already distinct; when each destination writes or clears the fields still needs to be investigated outward from the state file when the corresponding symptom occurs.

## The Retained Earlier Approach

"Look at end actions first" is not without value. If an anomaly occurs across multiple editing tools and only becomes apparent after actions are completed, end handling is still a reasonable starting point. The problem is that the old record mistakenly presented this starting point as a conclusion sufficient to rule out independent states, leading later investigators to look only for a unified reset without preserving the specific key sequence.

The additional visible changes mentioned in the early reports were not documented with reproducible visuals or input steps. That observation cannot distinguish lingering state from lingering tool results, nor can it show whether the issue occurs only in one particular tool. Because this original observation is itself incomplete, it can no longer be used to prove that Ctrl, Alt, and Alt+Shift should share the same state.

This record still contains the old judgment because it was once used as a starting point for release-period troubleshooting. Removing the initial draft would prevent those who later investigated end handling in the wrong direction from seeing the trade-offs made at the time. Preserving it while marking the premise overturned by the counterexample better serves the actual purpose of this material.

## Boundaries of the Current Decision

The current decision requires only this: when encountering a modifier-key anomaly in note editing, do not summarize every case as "modifier key stuck" anymore. Records should identify the stage at which it occurs and specify whether `ctrlHeld`, `altHeld`, or `altShiftHeld` is involved. Only then can individual keys, key combinations, and results remaining after editing ends be discussed separately.

The current decision does not require a new global state diagram for each field, nor does it claim that the three fields cover all input conditions. The local state in the file can serve as a starting point for investigation, but it cannot replace examination of a particular tool's input path. If the symptom appears in only one tool, first preserve the tool name and key sequence, then check its read sites near the state; only if multiple tools exhibit the same sequence is there reason to continue investigating shared end or reset handling.

Slicing transcription audio and multichannel trimming are outside the scope of this decision. That topic is retained separately in DOC-30; the correction to keyboard state on this page must not be extended into a judgment about audio interfaces.

The unconfirmed items remain: whether combination state is established by the order of key presses, supplied in advance by the input layer, or derived within editing state; whether the independent states are cleared in the same place or in different branches; and whether they resynchronize after focus loss. The old decision can no longer cover these questions, but the current review also lacks enough material to answer them.

# Proposal for Transcription Slicing and Multichannel Cropping

This page first captures the interface disagreement in the transcription-audio portion. The previous investigation found `OpenUtau.Core/Analysis/Some.cs` through `wave` and `audioslicer.slice`, but at the time that still wasn't enough to determine which layer was responsible for cropping, or which layer should convert multichannel audio to mono.

## The working hypothesis at the time

First have `audioslicer` perform `slice` based on the playback range, retain the returned `samples`, and then call `tomono` at analysis entry points that require mono. This way, frame calculation only deals with one well-defined sample buffer; if the channels are merged first, the cropping boundary may be reinterpreted by another layer.

Another option is to have the slicing API return a mono result directly. Its API surface for callers is smaller, but it would hide multichannel selection in the analysis entry point, and if the original channels need to be retained later, the migration cost would be higher. The first option is preferred for now, but there is not yet enough runtime evidence to support it.

## Parts to fill in

- Clarify whether the boundary of `wave` is based on the original samples or converted using `frame`.
- Use a stereo sample to verify the length and ordering of `samples` after `slice`.
- Confirm whether `tomono` should be a fixed step before analysis or belong only to a particular caller.

# Proposal for Transcription Slicing and Multichannel Trimming

This proposal originated with a case of "transcription runs, but the boundaries of the sliced audio are unclear." The first names encountered during the investigation were `wave`, `audioslicer`, and `audioslicer.slice`, so the old notes treated `OpenUtau.Core/Analysis/Some.cs` as the main entry point. It is indeed a useful place to revisit, but the path itself does not indicate that responsibility for slicing has been assigned here, nor that multichannel conversion happens here. For now, we are still examining direct adjacency for `internal/UTAU` at version `v_prev`, to avoid backfilling the early proposal with call relationships organized later.

## Assessments Retained in the Old Draft

The early draft described the processing order as follows: first use `slice` for the requested range, retain `samples` from the result, then call `tomono` where needed for analysis. The rationale at the time was straightforward: trimming should establish the time boundaries first, and channel merging should not change the interval to retrieve. The draft also retained an opposing view: if the slicing interface returns mono directly, callers will be simpler and test inputs will be easier to standardize.

These two approaches cannot both be treated as the established interface. The first order is friendlier to callers that need to preserve multiple channels, but it requires downstream consumers to know that `samples` may still contain multiple channels; the latter order reduces consumer-side branching, but may discard the original channel information at the entry point. The old draft did not provide enough examples to establish which of these costs had actually occurred, so "slice first, merge later" remains a candidate here, not a stable contract.

## Design Alternatives

**A: Return the original channels from slicing, then merge at the analysis entry point.**

`audioslicer.slice` is responsible only for extracting samples from the requested range. The `samples` in the return value retains the sliced result, and neither the channel count nor the layout is silently changed at this layer. Then call `tomono` before entering transcription analysis that requires mono input. The advantage of this alternative is that the division of responsibilities is easy to describe: slicing handles only time, and merging handles only channels; the cost is that every analysis caller must explicitly determine whether it needs mono and cannot guess from the return value's name.

**B: Have the slicing interface return mono directly.**

`slice` performs trimming and `tomono` internally, so analysis callers consume only one type of buffer. This alternative suits local paths with only mono analysis consumers, and the scope of changes appears smaller; however, if the multichannel input is needed for other analysis or diagnostics in the future, the original samples will no longer be in the returned result. It also combines "correct trimming boundaries" and "correct channel downmixing" into the same interface call, making it hard to distinguish which step caused a discrepancy when a failure occurs.

**C: Provide both results.**

Retain the original slice and provide a separate mono buffer. This approach is the most complete, but adds object fields and cache relationships; it should not be treated as the default design before confirming that both types of consumers actually exist. If adopted, it must be made clear whether the two results share the same boundaries, and whether callers are reading `samples` or another derived value; fields must not be added merely for "compatibility."

The current recommendation still leans toward A, but only for paths where it can be confirmed that callers explicitly need `tomono` before analysis. If investigation shows that all consumers require mono, B can be used as a local implementation; only if there are also consumers that preserve the original channels is there reason to continue evaluating C.

## What to Check on Re-examination

First, hold the same segment of `wave` input constant and vary only the channel count. Use the mono test case to confirm the length and start and end positions of `slice`; use the two-channel test case to confirm whether the layout of `samples` can still be recognized by callers. "Equal length" is not considered sufficient here, because interleaved and planar two-channel layouts can have the same total length yet be read differently during `tomono`.

Then hold the channel count fixed and vary only the trimming range. Compare against the conversion results from `frame`, and record whether the boundaries fall at the same sample positions; if the range comes from playback positions rather than raw sample indices, identify the layer where the conversion occurs. Finally, examine alternatives A and B separately: for A, confirm that merging takes place before the analysis entry point; for B, confirm that the interface does not silently discard channel information still needed by other callers before returning.

These checks address only interface behavior, not the quality of the model's analysis itself. Improvements or regressions in transcription results cannot be attributed directly to the trimming order unless the boundaries, channel count, and `samples` for the same input have all been recorded. There is currently no run output available to cite; this gap must remain acknowledged, and "slicing succeeded" cannot replace verification.

## Trade-offs from the Review

Before the review, the debate centered on "interface simplicity" versus "preserving raw data." Putting `tomono` into `slice` would shorten a single path, but the name would still suggest a pure trimming interface, making it hard for callers to realize that the data has changed. Separating the two steps is more verbose, but allows side paths that need the original multichannel data to continue reading it. Considering only the current transcription entry point, B may require less code; if future audio diagnostics are also taken into account, A has a smaller rollback scope.

The follow-up card UTA-217 requested that the run records for "Transcription Audio Slicing and Multichannel Trimming" be completed. By the later re-examination, the relevant implementation had already been completed on an existing branch, and the material went straight into review; this shows that there were code changes available to inspect, but does not by itself establish which of alternatives A, B, or C had been verified. The actual inputs and outputs should still be added to this page or the corresponding test records before review approval.

## Withdrawal Criteria and Open Issues

If the two-channel test case shows that A's `tomono` reads the wrong layout, withdraw the "slice first, then merge" order and pause to verify the channel layout; do not recast the issue as a boundary problem. If range conversion causes `frame` to produce different sample endpoints for the same request, withdraw the assumption that boundaries can be determined directly at the `slice` layer, and go back to check the conversion from playback positions to sample positions. If B has already been adopted but there are still consumers that need the original channels, restore access to the original slice instead of having callers guess the channels again.

Still unresolved are the actual handoff relationships within `OpenUtau.Core/Analysis/Some.cs` involving `wave`, `audioslicer.slice`, and `samples`, as well as the exact call boundary of `tomono`. This remains the entry point for investigation; do not let the proposal's conclusions speak for the implementation prematurely.

A later review of the original records showed that the old state had not been replaced by the subsequent recovery actions, so "it worked later" could not explain the earlier discrepancy.

## Incident timeline

| Relative time | Observation | Action taken at the time |
|---|---|---|
| T+00 | Two states first appeared for the same object | Saved the original records and the page entry point at the time |
| T+07 | A set of plugin call samples was still available | Narrowed the scope to adaptation and integration feedback, without broadening it to a system-wide issue |
| T+18 | Subsequent comparisons did not eliminate the difference between the two revisions | Stopped sending repeated requests and retained the comparison points |
| T+31 | The call path recovered | Recorded recovery separately from the assessment of the cause |

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Seen: Dual states detected
    Seen --> Preserved: Original records retained
    Preserved --> Compared: Compared the two observation times
    Compared --> Restored: Call path recovered
    Compared --> Open: Cause unconfirmed
    Open --> Compared: Additional records obtained
```

Recovery only shows that the call path was working again at that time. It does not show that the two states originally represented the same revision, nor that the change in the project tick has been explained. What could be restored during the incident was the sampling frame; there is still no record tying the project tick change to a cause. This distinction was not made clear in the first write-up, making it easy for readers to mistake the page showing recovery for a root cause explanation.

The earlier accounts based only on screenshots did not help either. A screenshot can prove that a particular state was seen, but the screenshots did not preserve the sequence linking the two states; they cannot explain why the other record still showed the old revision. No later attempt was made to fill in the missing window from memory; the unobserved parts remained blank.

This page covers only the call samples, adaptation boundaries, and integration feedback around the plugin. These have their own schedules, maintainers, and exit criteria; speculation about adjacent projects was not included in the causal analysis. If you need to revisit the incident, start at `docs/adj-openutau/incidents/OpenUtau-client-integration-two-states-for-one-object.md`.

Outstanding items: fill in the times before and after the state transition; verify the records corresponding to each of the two revisions; clarify whether the project tick change affects only the display or also the call samples. The call path recovery has been recorded; the cause remains open.
